## R297 — The fifteen are a REVIEW, not a confirmation, and my "no new judgement" was wrong
*David's question, 2026-08-19: does a published tier on an already-authored judgement need a fresh read?*

**A FRESH REVIEW, and the rows say so themselves:**

- `authoredBy: ai-draft:cowork-okafor-v1` — **the tier was drafted by a machine.**
- `preReviewVerdict: PASS_TO_HUMAN` — the draft pipeline's own verdict is that a person must look.
- **ZERO attribution events across all 183 DRAFT vault rows.** No human has ever signed one.

So *"the judgement exists"* is true only in the sense that a draft carries a number. **Nobody has
judged it.** I wrote **"no new judgement"** about this work and it was wrong: publishing a
machine-drafted tier IS the judgement, made for the first time.

**AND THE READ IS WIDER THAN THE TIER.** Each row carries `definitionChild` and `sentence`, both
child-facing and both served on the Word card. **Fifteen reads of three child-facing fields each,
not fifteen confirmations** — and the pack already found one blocking fault: `futile`'s definition
reads *"certain to fail"*, and **fail is banned child-facing under D1.**

**THE REUSABLE FORM: "already authored" is not a claim about a PERSON until a person is named.** A
populated field and a made decision look identical in a table, and the difference is an attribution
event. The whole R94/R271 thread is this same distinction — here it arrived as a work estimate,
where the wrong answer would have converted fifteen reviews into fifteen rubber stamps.

## R298 — The vault covers stems and not keys: fifteen publications buy ONE measurable pair
*Measured 2026-08-19, correcting a claim I made and David repeated.*

measurable. MEASURED: it turns ONE.**

| of the 40 bank pairs | |
|---|---:|
| both sides have a vault entry | **1** |
| stem only | **39** |
| key only | 0 |
| neither | 0 |

**All 40 stems have entries. Exactly one KEY does — `brave`, and it is only there because it is

ABOUT and not the words items ANSWER WITH. **No number of stem publications can fix that**, and

**THE ERROR SHAPE: I COUNTED THE POPULATION I HAD JUST MEASURED AND ASSUMED IT WAS THE ONE THAT
MATTERED.** Fifteen unpublished stem tiers is a true and useful number; *fifteen measurable pairs*
is a different quantity that happens to share its size, and I carried the first across into the
second without re-deriving it. **A pair needs two sides and I checked one** — R249's family
(errors in what is being counted, not in the arithmetic), now on its fourth instance.

**no threshold set or defaulted** — she sets it after seeing the distribution.

## R299 — Where every default is wrong, refuse
*David, 2026-08-19, on the undeclared-type refusal. Worth its own line.*

`stem.words[]` carries headwords, components and set-members. An undeclared word-bearing type
**fails the run** rather than falling to either side, because **both defaults are wrong in opposite
directions**: guess `components` and a vocabulary family silently leaves the tier rule's scope;
guess `headword-under-test` and a compound bank is blocked over words nobody would tier.

**The general form: a default is a decision made in advance by whoever wrote the code, on behalf of
a case they have not seen.** Where the cases genuinely differ in kind, that decision cannot be
right, and the honest move is to make the next person state which kind they have. It is the same
instinct as `declareMayBeEmpty` (R61) and `requirePopulation` — **a silence that has to be broken
before the run continues.**

## R300 — Don't re-derive from code, from a proxy, or from what the data states
*David, 2026-08-19: the third form closes the set.*

Three ways to re-derive a property someone has already established, all now seen:

1. **From code** (R41) — the M-column recompute reimplemented "across-zero" instead of calling the
   family's own `subInfo`, and reported 69 disagreements against a signed sheet, every one
   manufactured.
2. **From a proxy** (R290) — "has no space" stood in for "is a headword", so every single-word value
   anywhere got the same free pass, and my replacement field list was another proxy.
3. **From what the data itself states** (R295) — the quote window split an extract on newlines, 32
   of them, against **83 declared `numberedLines`**, and reported eleven LIVE quotes as
   out-of-window. Every one was the instrument.

**A file that declares a property should be ASKED, not MEASURED.** The three share one cause: a
derivation is cheaper to write than a lookup, and it is wrong in a way that looks like a finding.
**All three produced confident numbers about content that was fine** — which is why the rule is
worth stating as a set rather than as three incidents.

## R307 — Only the banned clause moves
*David's rule, 2026-08-19, from the `futile` fix.*

A gate-held child-facing string is repaired by **changing only what the gate refuses.** `futile`'s
definition lost *fail* and kept everything else.

**A wholesale redraft would have put my authoring in front of the reviewer under a machine's name,
and she would have been reviewing me while believing she was reviewing the draft.** That is worse
than the original fault: the fault was one banned word a scanner catches, and the substitution is an
undetectable change of author inside a review.

**And the pack rule beside it: a read pack must never carry a blocker the gate already found.** The
gate exists to clear mechanical faults so a reviewer's time goes on the judgements only she can
make. **A pack containing a known blocker is a gate failure dressed as a review request.**

It is a dismiss, so it is named as one: **`Close`**. The test id moves with it (`walk-close`), and

## R311 — The definition house style: a gloss, not a sentence
*David's ruling, 2026-08-19, taking Annie's preference as house style.*

**A lower-case fragment with no terminal stop**, because the card reads as **a gloss under a
headword** — the headword is already there and the definition completes it, so sentence-casing a
completion makes one card read as two statements.

**Applied across all 301 rows: 157 changed** (118 LIVE, 39 DRAFT); 144 were already in house style.
Lengths ran 1 to 18 words, median 8.

**IT IS A REGISTER CHANGE AND THE APPLIER ASSERTS THAT BEFORE WRITING.** Only the first character's
case and a trailing stop move; every row is checked to be identical once case and terminal
punctuation are normalised, and the run refuses on any row where it is not. **So a reviewer
comparing before and after checks one property rather than re-reading 157 definitions** — the same
discipline as the `futile` fix (R307). Proper nouns and *I* keep their capital: lower-casing them
would be a spelling error dressed as a house style.

## R314 — All 32 held, and holding a card does not stop its item serving
*Annie's ruling generalised, 2026-08-19: do not publish a Word card whose definition contains the
key of any item it serves.*

**32 findings, 20 distinct cards held, 12 of them LIVE.** Not the eight she read.

**WHAT A HOLD DOES, MEASURED FROM THE SERVING CODE RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** `collectCards` reads the
`Word` table where status is LIVE; items read `Item`. **There is no join between them at serving
time.** So a hold removes the card from the vault collect pool and from the word-review distractor
pool, **and does not stop the vocabulary item serving** — the 15 LIVE items keep running.

**AND THAT IS THE SAFE DIRECTION, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH STATING.** The leak runs card → item: a
child who has collected the card can answer from memory. **Withdrawing the card closes the leak and
leaves the question intact.** A child in the meantime meets the item *without having been handed its
answer*, which is what the item was written to ask. Holding the ITEM instead would have removed a
sound question to fix a card.

**HELD AT THE DOOR, NOT DEMOTED BY STATUS** (the R208 shape). A card's status records a REVIEW
decision; a hold records a SERVING one. These cards were properly approved **for what they say** and
are withdrawn **for what they reveal**, and collapsing the two would lose that distinction on the
row.

## R319 — Not two ban lists: one rule and a pattern bug on my side
*David, 2026-08-19: the emitting side cannot reproduce your refusal, so it cannot fix it.*

`ENG-015-CC-12` was refused for **"behind"** on *"he looks behind the door"*. Cowork bans `behind`
only in the falling-behind stance — **and so do I.** The rule is the same on both sides. **My
implementation over-matched.**

One branch read `(you|he|she|they|we) … (is|are|was|were|feel|look|looks|seem) … behind` with **no
constraint on what follows**, so a rule written for *"she is behind"* caught *"he looks behind the
door"*. **The emitting store could not reproduce the refusal because there was nothing to reproduce.**

**Fixed:** the copula branch requires `behind` to END the clause — a progress *behind* takes no
object — and perception verbs leave that branch, being direction rather than progress. Eleven
fixtures; **no serving row changed**; `ENG-015-CC-12` now imports.

**THE TRANSFERABLE HALF: A REFUSAL THE OTHER SIDE CANNOT REPRODUCE IS A CLAIM ABOUT MY INSTRUMENT,
NOT ABOUT THEIR CONTENT.** Six weeks of that item sitting outside the store, and the diagnostic was
available the moment someone asked *"can you reproduce this?"* — which nothing in the exchange
required either side to ask. The list is now emitted with every pattern and band so the comparison
can be made rather than assumed.

## R320 — Quoted spans exempt, per field, refusing where undeclared — and it unblocks nothing
*David's ruling, 2026-08-19.*

**A quotation records what a source says; changing it to satisfy our house rules makes the record
false** — and Annie has already ruled these source-of-truth fields, checked by exact match (R291).
A field cannot be both *"must match the source exactly"* and *"must obey our spelling"* when the
source is an American novel of 1903.

Built on `attractorQuote`, `defeaterQuote` and declared passage spans. **Undeclared refuses**
(R299). **Narrow by design:** it lifts the BAN LIST and the US-SPELLING check — rules about OUR
VOICE — and lifts neither the reading-age cap nor the long-word ceiling nor the id-leak rule, which
are rules about **what a child can read**. A quotation is not our voice; it is exactly as hard to
read as any other sentence.

**AND IT UNBLOCKS ZERO OF THE FIVE, WHICH IS THE FINDING.** All five refusals sit in AUTHORED fields
— four in `walkScript`, one in `option.value`. **But four are quotations EMBEDDED INSIDE an authored
field**: *…line 3 answers the stem: **'Mr. Jeremiah Cobb was favoring the horses as much'**.*

**The mechanism for that already exists and the items do not use it.** `checkChildFacingText`
accepts `quotedSpans`; declaring the span clears the refusal — verified, 1 fault undeclared, 0
declared. **So the fix is neither a reword nor a field exemption: it is the item declaring the span
it is already quoting.** A field-level exemption cannot reach a quotation inside a sentence, and
noticing that is the difference between shipping the ruling and shipping something that looks like
it.

`ENG-023-RT-08` is the exception: *"with fibers"* is an OPTION VALUE, our wording, so `fibres` is a
genuine correction.

## R321 — Eight refusals the exemption does not touch, and why that is correct
*2026-08-19.*

Four on sentence length (`ENG-001-WIW-03`, `-14`, `-18`, `ENG-002-pp-17`) and four on long words or
the library (`ENG-002-pp-19`, `ENG-004-AGG-03`, `-08`, `ENG-014-TS-10`). **The quoted-span exemption
touches none of them, by design.**

The line is worth stating because it will be asked again: **the exemption lifts rules about OUR
VOICE and never rules about A CHILD'S READING.** We may not impose our spelling on Kate Douglas
Wiggin — but a 24-word sentence is 24 words whoever wrote it, and a child meeting it in a quotation
is in exactly the position she would be in meeting it in ours. **A quotation is a defence against a
house-style rule and never against a comprehension one.**

All eight remain outstanding on their own merits, and all eight are still going out.

## R322 — `ENG-019-BV-02`: the banned word is the object of study
*Escalated to Annie, 2026-08-19.*

The stem asks **why Bevis says *"There, if you had run quick!"*** — so `quick` is **what the item is
about**. There is no wording to change without changing the question.

**A span declaration would clear the gate, and that is precisely why it must not be applied without
her.** The question is not *can we exempt this string* — the machinery would, silently and
immediately. It is **whether an item may quote a banned word as its subject**, which is a decision
about what the product is willing to put in front of a child in order to teach about it.

**The easy availability of the technical answer is the reason to be careful**, not a reason to
proceed: the gate would go green and nobody would ever be asked.

## R323 — Direction declared per bank, because the same number means opposite things
*Annie's ruling, 2026-08-19, before any frequency measurement runs.*

**`vr-04`'s construct is decode-the-hard-word**, so a key rarer than its stem is a fault — the item
has asked the child to decode twice. **`vr-21`'s construct is recognise-the-rarer-synonym**, so the
identical relation is the point.

**Without the declaration a frequency signal reads against no stated expectation**, and would
condemn one bank and endorse another for the same measurement. **That is worse than no signal: a
number with no direction looks like evidence and is a coin toss.** It is the R263 shape in
measurement clothes — a property judged by the instance it was first observed on.

Declared in `bank-direction.ts`, **beside the construct it is a fact about**, and an undeclared bank
returns null so the caller stops rather than guessing (R299).

**AND vr-16 IS REPORTED AS A MEASUREMENT, WHICH IS THAT IT CANNOT BE MADE.** Its construct is
antonymy, where difficulty may sit in the RELATION rather than in either word's rarity — a genuine
question, not an oversight. **24 of its 25 pairs have no card for the key**, so the tier signal
reports on one. Named in `UNDECLARED_BANKS` with that reason. **An honest "not measurable" is a
finding; a guessed direction would have been a fabrication with a number attached.**

## R326 — The recognition test is staged, not judged
*Annie's narrowed standard, 2026-08-19.*

**Not "does the card answer the item in different words" but "does answering from the card require
any step beyond recognition?"** The narrowing matters: a card that makes a child hold two senses
apart is doing the item's teaching; a card she can recognise the answer in is doing its work.

40 LIVE items joined to a card: **19 already held for a string match, 21 for her judgement alone.**
Flagged cases sort first so the read starts where the faults are.

**NOT JUDGED HERE, AND THE REASON IS THE RULING ITSELF.** She says it is answerable by a reader in
seconds. **A machine judging it would substitute a string test for the judgement she named** — which
is precisely the substitution that produced 32 findings where she had found 8, and precisely the one
that cannot find the 33rd.

## R328 — Nothing screens a passage for suitability, and 26 written judgements are unread
*Reported, not proposed, 2026-08-19. Confirmed independently against Cowork.*

**Six checks read `content/passages` — line refs, cloze gaps, verbatim integrity, source quotes,
serving path, and the vocabulary scan. Not one screens content for suitability.**

**26 ban-list rules, ZERO protective**, matching Cowork's count exactly. No rule mentions race,
violence, slurs, harm or period attitude. **The list is a VOICE list** — it bans *fail*, *wrong*,
*weak*, *guarantee*, *learning style* — built to keep our tone right, and never to keep a child
safe. Those are different jobs and only one of them has ever been done.

**AND THE NEAR-MISS IS THE SHARPEST PART.** `contentFlags` exists on **26 of 29 passages**, carrying
authored prose exactly on this subject — a horse falling on ice, a girl alone at dusk with a strange
man, a comic metaphor about slaughtering innocents — **each with a Recommendation.** **Nothing reads
the field.** Twenty-six considered judgements about content suitability, written down by whoever
curated the passages, and no code path opens them.

**It is the retirement-with-no-reader fault (R269) on the most consequential field yet**, and it is
**the first gap this project has found by ASKING rather than by breaking.** No list authored: what
the product will and will not serve is a governance decision, David's with Annie's reading behind
it.

## R329 — 62 undeclared quotations: a future refusal and an unverified quote at once
*Annie's §4, measured 2026-08-19.*

**62 undeclared quotations across 48 items, 12 on LIVE items** — 33 in `walkScript`, 26 in
`stem.text`, 3 in `hintCore` — against **33 spans already declared.** The mechanism is used on about
a third of what it covers.

**Each is two problems wearing one shape.** It **refuses the next time a rule tightens** — `favoring`
sat in a walkScript for weeks and became a refusal only when the US-spelling rule reached that
field, so every undeclared quotation is a future refusal waiting on an unrelated change. **And
nothing verifies it against the source**, because `check:source-quotes` reads only the fields Annie
named, so an embedded quotation can drift from its passage silently — the exact fault that check
exists to catch elsewhere.

**The mechanism has existed all along and is unused.** Declaring the span both exempts it from our
house rules and brings it under the source check. **Nothing was missing but the declaration**, which
is the third time this month a fix has turned out to be a field nobody filled in.

## R331 — The 62 spans declared, and the claim made true rather than softened
*Annie's §4, applied 2026-08-19.*

**49 items gained 62 span declarations. No text moved** — not one character of any stem, hint or
walk script. A declaration is a statement ABOUT text that is already there, so a reviewer comparing
before and after sees the same words with a record attached. Undeclared quotations: **62 → 0.**

**AND I DESCRIBED IT AS TURNING A FUTURE REFUSAL INTO A *VERIFIED* QUOTATION, WHICH WAS HALF UNTRUE
WHEN WRITTEN.** `check:source-quotes` read only `attractorQuote` and `defeaterQuote`, so the 62 new
spans were **exempted from our house rules and verified against the passage by nothing.**

**An exemption without a verification is strictly worse than neither**: the text stops being
screened for our rules and gains no check that it still matches its source. The check now reads
`explanation.quotes` too — **1053 quotes checked, up from 980** — so the claim is true rather than
softened in prose.

**THE BACKLOG WENT 30 → 31 AND THE CONTENT DID NOT CHANGE: THE POPULATION DID.** One of the newly
covered spans cites text outside its item's `lineRefs`. **A backlog that grows because the
denominator grew is a different event from one that grows because content got worse**, and the
constant carries that reason — recording the number alone would have made the two indistinguishable
the next time somebody read it. R62's discipline on a threshold rather than on a report.

## R332 — 61 flags on 26 passages, two of them reachable, and nobody recorded who judged
*Emitted for Annie, 2026-08-19. No check built, deliberately.*

**THE FIGURE CARRIED IN WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED: 26 PASSAGES CARRYING 61 FLAGS**, not 26 flags.
`stream-b-01` carries three.

**AND ONLY TWO PASSAGES ARE REACHABLE BY A CHILD TODAY** — `stream-a-03-wind-in-willows` (22 LIVE
items) and `stream-b-01` (12), both REACHABLE(free). The other 27 sit behind DRAFT items. **So 61
judgements exist and six of them govern anything a child can meet.** That is the scoping fact the
raw count hides.

**WHAT NOBODY RECORDED:** no field names who authored a flag; no timestamp; **zero attribution
events for `recordType: 'Passage'` in the whole store**; and no code path reads the field. The
judgements are real, considered, and anonymous.

**THE THREE UNFLAGGED PASSAGES ARE NOT ONE CASE.** Two are the ENG-003 cloze vehicles —
commissioned originals, *"not adapted from any source"* — where flagging nothing is plausible.
**The third is `stream-a-02-railway-children`: E. Nesbit, 1906, curated from Gutenberg, and the only
ADAPTED CLASSIC in the store with no content flag at all** when all 26 of its peers have one. That

**NO CHECK BUILT, ON DAVID'S RULING AND IT IS THE right one.** A check over flags whose standard is
unstated would **enforce whatever the flags happen to say — turning one curator's unrecorded
judgement into the product's policy by the act of automating it.** The standard is the thing that
does not exist, and a mechanism cannot supply it.

## R334 — `railway-children` goes to her UNJUDGED, which is not the same artefact as CLEAN
*David's ruling, 2026-08-19: do not flag it.*

**THREE PASSAGES CARRY NO FLAGS AND THEY ARE THREE DIFFERENT STATES.** The two cloze vehicles have
**no `contentFlags` field at all**; `stream-a-02-railway-children` has the field **present and
empty**. The other 26 are populated. **An empty array is what a curator writes having looked and
found nothing, AND what a template writes having never been filled**, and it is the only adapted
classic in that state.

**EVERY OTHER ASSESSMENT THE PASSAGE COULD CARRY, IT CARRIES, AND ALL PASS**: copyright (PD from
1995), similarity (112 papers, 943 shingles, no hits), verbatim (26 of 26 spans, 100%), band
(ratified). **And `curationNotes` is substantial and entirely about FIT** — the scene was chosen
over the red-petticoat episode because that one cannot be cut to the word band without losing the
landslide or the rescue. **A recorded judgement about length and shape, silent on content.**

**THE INFERENCE IS STATED AS INFERENCE.** That every neighbour is recorded and this one is empty is
**evidence, not proof** — consistent with a curator who screened a gentle domestic scene and found
nothing, and equally consistent with a field nobody reached. **`editorialCuts` is `[]` too, and
there the empty array IS corroborated** by *"needs no cuts at all"* in the note. **No such sentence
exists for content**, and that asymmetry is the closest thing to a finding available.

**Twelve items cite it, `ENG-008-RC-01`–`12`, all DRAFT, none reachable.** So it is worth resolving
now rather than urgently: **before publication the cost is a reading; after publication it is a
withdrawal.**

**Not flagged, because flagging it would BE the judgement.** If it was never judged it needs a first
one; if it was judged it needs the record nobody wrote. **Both are the same act by her and neither
is available to anyone else.**

## R335 — No parser: a shape problem underneath a standard problem
*David's ruling, 2026-08-19.*

The 61 flags come in two shapes — **16 structured** (`{element, recommendation, reason}`) and
**45 prose** (*"…Recommendation: keep. It is brief comic rudeness…"*). A parser is the obvious next
build and it is the wrong one.

**Parsing `Recommendation: keep` today would silently miss the next author**, who will write
*"Recommend keeping"* or put the verdict first — and the parser would report that flag as having no
recommendation, or worse, as having none needed. **A shape problem underneath a standard problem
resolves in that order**: the standard says what a flag must state, and the shape follows from it.
Building the parser first fixes the shape to whatever the flags happen to look like now, which is
the same fault as building the check — **automation converting one curator's habit into the
product's grammar.**

**2026-08-19. Annie, vr-04 closest-meaning bank. Asked four times before it was done.**

`bank-vr-04-closest-meaning-30` (exhausted) takes **`worn out`**, replacing `tired`.
Authored by Annie, applied through the written-review path, `reviewedBy: reviewer:rev-0001`.

key-commoner-than-stem, and that is UNVERIFIED for both replacements: neither has a vault entry and
no frequency source is installed (SUBLEX-UK remains UNESTABLISHED, not refused — the enquiry is
drafted and unsent). The row carries the qualifier and the **return condition**: these keys go back
to Annie the day a frequency signal lands, and if either is still rarer than its stem she chooses

**The rule this instances: a provisional value with a named return condition is a decision; the same
value without one is a guess that will be read as a decision.** R203's placement applies — the
qualifier is in the field (`provisionalAgainstDirection`, `r4Note`), never one field over in prose.

**Two improvements were deliberately NOT made, and both are hers, not mine.** `tired` is not added as
a `vr04-wrong-strength` distractor on `-30`; `well-behaved` being the only hyphenated option among

fault, and each would re-derive a LIVE reviewed item — the coupling R62 refuses. Routed to their own

## R337 — A declared quoted span counts as ONE unit against the sentence cap, not zero

**2026-08-19. Annie, every district.** Implemented on the **span declaration**, never on quotation
marks — a rule keyed on punctuation hands the exemption to anyone who types an apostrophe, and the
62 spans declared under R335 are what make it checkable at all.

Previously a declared span was **stripped entirely** and counted as zero, which flattered the number
in the other direction. It now collapses to a single word-shaped token, so a 22-word stem carrying a
14-word quotation measures 9 — not 22, and not 8.

**The vocabulary ceiling still removes the span completely**, unchanged and deliberately different: a
hard word inside a quotation is the source's, and we are not answerable for Grahame's vocabulary.
Two caps, two treatments of the same span, because they are asking different questions — the
sentence cap asks how much a child must hold at once (a quotation is one thing to hold), the
vocabulary ceiling asks what we chose to put in front of her (nothing, if it is quoted).

**What it unblocks today: NOTHING, and the zero is the finding.** Of the 25 items failing
sentence-length store-wide, **zero carry a declared span** — the rule only reaches a quotation that
has been declared, and the failing items are not among the 113 items now carrying declarations.
Its value is **entirely prospective**, which is not the same as a rule that does nothing, and saying
so plainly is what stops a true zero being read as a failed ruling (R60).

## R338 — The long-word ceiling counts distinct headwords, not tokens

**2026-08-19. Annie, every district.** `imagination` / `imagining` share a root and are **one**
demand on a child. `ordinary` inside `extraordinary` is **one** hard word — and on `ENG-004-AGG-08`
removing either would delete the question, which is built on the contrast between them.

**Counting tokens made the gate measure REPETITION, which costs a child nothing, instead of VARIETY,
which is the entire point of a vocabulary ceiling.** A stem that uses one hard word four times was
scored as four times the load of a stem using it once, and a stem using four different hard words
scored the same as both.

Implemented as conservative root-grouping plus a containment rule (a shorter word wholly inside a
longer one is the same demand; the longer is kept). The failure detail reports **both** figures —
*"2 distinct long word(s) … counted from 4 token(s)"* — so a reviewer sees the rule operating rather
than inferring it from a number that moved.

**Store-wide it unblocks one item** (long-words failures 3 → 2 in the DRAFT backlog, 1 remaining
store-wide).

**And it exposed a test that was asserting the wrong thing.** `item-content-gate.test.ts` carried a
case named for the undeclared-span rule and proved it with **the exact `ordinary`/`extraordinary`
pair this ruling is about** — so the test was encoding the token count, not the exemption rule in
its own name, and only by accident. R263: the ruling is about the property, not the string it was
first observed on. The fixture now uses two genuinely distinct long words, preserving the test's
stated intent, and a second case asserts the pair counts as one.

## R339 — Converging the sentence cap: the arithmetic decides nothing, the declaration decides everything

**2026-08-20. Cowork's gate strips a declared span before counting; ours counts it as one unit
(R337). Asked to converge or say why not.**

**Converge — and the direction is Cowork adopting ours**, because Annie's ruling explicitly overturned
strip-to-zero as *"flattering the number the other way"*, and a gate quietly reverting a three-day-old
reviewer decision is what R62 refuses. **We WERE Cowork's rule until 19 August**; this is not two
designs meeting, it is one design that got a ruling with the other store holding the pre-ruling
version.

**Measured over all 90 texts carrying a declared span: 0 verdict differences, and 0 texts at the band
where a difference could exist.** The two rules can disagree in exactly one circumstance — our own
wording at *precisely* 16 words with a span alongside. At 15 both pass, at 17 both fail. **The
disagreement has nowhere to stand.** Adopting therefore costs nothing today, and the band is one word
wide, so it will bite.

**AND THE ARITHMETIC IS NOT WHAT FORCED THE REWORD, WHICH IS THE FINDING.** Both stores stripped
spans identically on 17 August — *the same rule* — so the cap rule cannot explain a disagreement on
that date. **It was the DECLARATION.** Four texts in this store have their verdict decided by the
declaration alone, swinging 11–14 words: `ENG-001-WIW-14` (8 declared / 22 undeclared, **LIVE**),
`ENG-002-pp-17` (7/19), `ENG-003-A-CZ-A1` (6/20), `ENG-003-A-CZ-B1` (6/17). Cowork held a declaration
we did not; **both gates were correct and were reading different rows.**

**So converging the RULE converges an arithmetic that changes nothing, and converging the DECLARATION
SETS is what stops the gates disagreeing.** No mechanism compares them in either direction — R88's
return leg in different clothes. Requested from Cowork alongside the rule: its declaration set as item
id, field and span text.

**Correction to R337's own report.** I wrote that the cap ruling *"unblocks nothing today"*. True of
R337, and wrong to leave standing alone: **the declarations (R331) unblocked four texts, one LIVE.**
The two landed in the same act and will be remembered as one. **The declaration is the mechanism that
does the work; the counting rule only says what to do once it is there.**

## R340 — The content standard has to cover what is never chosen, not only what is cut

**David's, 2026-08-20, arising from the eight removals in Cowork's `activeRemovalsForContent`.**

**All eight carry an avoidance**; four ALSO carry a cut; **none is a cut alone**. **Five** name
racial or ethnic content. All eight sit in a manifest field **with no author and no date**.

**Both of those figures correct my own first count**, which said "six of the eight are avoidances,
not cuts" and "four name racial or ethnic content". The error was reading the entries as a summary
instead of marking each against both limbs: Tom Sawyer and Eighty Days were filed as avoidance-only
when both say *"cut"* in their own text, and Mill on the Floss's ethnic slur was missed entirely.
**The avoidance limb is not a subset here, it is universal**, which sharpens this entry rather than
softening it — and the correction only surfaced because the delivery marks the split PER ENTRY,
which a prose summary of the same eight had not forced anyone to do.

**A cut and an avoidance are different acts and only one of them has a subject.** A cut changes a
passage a child reads, and something remains to inspect. **An avoidance decides which passage exists
at all — so it is invisible to every gate we have, because the gates read what is there.** It is
closer to a commissioning policy than to a content flag, and it currently has no record of who
decided it or against what.

**The standard, when written, must therefore cover both limbs** — what may be cut from a passage, and
what may cause a passage not to be chosen — and the second has the larger consequences and the weaker
record. Annie's two conditions point the same way and are adopted as scope: **it must cover the
corpus we might ADD rather than only the one we hold**, and **it must name who may judge**.

**This is David's to write, with Annie's reading. Nothing here authors it**, and the standing
instruction not to author a protective list is unchanged — recording the required SCOPE is not
drafting the standard, and the distinction is the point.

## R341 — The declaration-set comparison, opened as its own thread; and the four are only the boundary cases

**David's instruction, 2026-08-20, opening D3.** `pnpm check:declaration-sets`. Both stores gate on a
DECLARED quoted span and neither can see the other's declarations. It compares item id, field and span
text, **in both directions**, and runs itself when Cowork's set arrives.

**THE FOUR FROM R339 ARE NOT THE POPULATION — THEY ARE THE ONES THAT HAPPEN TO SIT AT A CAP
BOUNDARY.** A divergence on a comfortably short sentence passes on both sides today and is no less a
divergence; the two gates agree **by sentence length, not by rule**. So every divergence is reported
and each is classified: `ACTIVE` (a verdict differs today) or `LATENT` (agrees for no reason). **A
latent divergence becomes active the day someone edits the sentence** — an ordinary thing to do to a
stem — and nothing would connect that edit to the refusal that follows.

**Three classes, because a one-directional diff misses the third:** declared here and absent there,
declared there and absent here, and **same item and field with different span text** — the worst of
the three, because both stores believe they have declared the same thing.

**CORRECTED 2026-08-20: THE THIRD CLASS WAS ITSELF ONE-WAY, WHICH IS THE FAULT IT EXISTS TO CATCH,
ONE LEVEL UP.** Asked to confirm the class was in the check, I read the code rather than answering
from what I had written, and found it compared span text FROM OUR SIDE ONLY. A span **Cowork**
declares on a field we also declare — where every one of our own spans matches theirs — fell through
every filter: not absent-there (they hold the key), not absent-here (we hold it), not
different-text (our spans were all present in theirs). **A field both stores declare is exactly
where a one-way read looks complete.** Now a set difference on span text in BOTH directions, per
field, reported as four classes rather than three. Fault-injected with that precise case: the old
code reported 0 divergences, the new code reports 1.

**It fails on ACTIVE and reports on LATENT.** An active divergence means one store is refusing an
item the other serves, which is a present fault. A latent one needs Cowork to act, and a step red
from a queue we cannot clear is muted within a week (`check:staging-queue`'s finding).

**It prints NOT RECEIVED, never "0 divergences"** (R60). A comparison with one side missing asserts
nothing, and the only wrong thing that run could do is print a number that reads like agreement.
**Our 157 declarations export on every run** so the return leg travels whether or not theirs has
(R88) — the comparison is never blocked on both sides at once.

**AND THE FAULT INJECTION FOUND A REAL BUG IN THE CHECK, WHICH IS THE ENTRY'S POINT.** Four faults
were planted, one per class plus a known-ACTIVE and a known-LATENT; all four were found. But one was
labelled **"TEXT NOT IN THIS STORE"** for an item that is plainly in the store. The reader took
`container.text`, and **`explanation` has no `text` key** — its child-facing strings are `hintCore`
and `walkScript` — so every explanation-side declaration was reported as a missing item.

**That is a claim about the STORE reporting a fact about my READ: R173's exact shape, committed
inside the check written to close the divergence R339 found.** Nothing but the injection would have
caught it, because the wrong label sat beside three correctly-found faults and the run as a whole
agreed with what I expected — R173's transferable half, that a confirming result has to be
investigated on purpose.

**The repair is to stop naming fields at all:** `consequenceOf` now takes the whole container and
calls the gate's own `textsFrom` (R41 — a verifier states its source; R57 — never re-list the fields
a door reads), skipping `_previous*` history. The two labels are now distinct facts: `ITEM NOT IN
THIS STORE` versus `SPAN IN NO TEXT ON THIS CONTAINER`.

## R342 — Five artefacts reported as sent were `cp`ed past the delivery door, and two of them never existed as separate files

**David, 2026-08-20. Two artefacts reported as sent had not arrived, and the arrival rule applies:
staged is not crossed (R255).**

**They were not even staged properly.** `deliver()` copies, hashes the staged BYTES, writes a
`.sha256` sidecar and counts the queue. I used `cp` and `writeFileSync`, which does the copy and
none of the rest. Every correctly-staged artefact in the outbound folder carries a sidecar; my five
carried none — so there was **no digest for Cowork to quote back**, which is the only way arrival is
ever confirmed. **The mechanism existed, was written for exactly this, and I went around it.**

**And I wrote "Delivered" and "sent".** Both are claims this side cannot make. `deliver()` prints
`STAGED` and says so in its own output; writing something stronger than the tool's own word is the
record running ahead of the act.

**THE SECOND FAULT IS SIMPLER AND WORSE: TWO ARTEFACTS WERE ONE FILE.** The eight removals were
appended to the flag file, so an instruction to send two things produced one, and a reader looking
for the second found nothing rather than finding it misplaced. **An absent artefact and an absent
path are the same thing** (R88) — a reader cannot discover what was folded into something else.

**A third, found while repairing the first two: `check:declaration-sets` had the same fault**, one
day old. It wrote its export straight into the outbound folder with `writeFileSync`. Now built to
`content/exports/` and staged through `deliver()` like everything else.

**What the repaired delivery adds, beyond the digests.** The flag file now carries **both passages
complete and asserted complete** — the build compares emitted text to source and fails on any
difference. Annie reads a flag against the passage it describes, so a flag file without the text is
a verdict with the evidence withheld; it can be agreed with but not CHECKED. And the eight removals
are marked **per entry** for cut versus avoidance rather than summarised underneath.

**Marking per entry corrected the summary twice** — see R340. Both errors survived a prose summary
of the same eight sentences and died the moment each entry had to be marked individually. **That is
the argument for per-entry marking, not a footnote to it.**

## R343 — A directory the other side reads needs a guard on what ENTERS it, not only on what changes

**David's ruling, 2026-08-20, after R342.** `pnpm check:outbound-sidecars`.

**`cp` into the outbound folder was indistinguishable from a delivery, and the only tell was a
missing sidecar that nothing read.** `deliver()` copies, hashes the staged BYTES, writes a `.sha256`
sidecar and counts the queue; a `cp` does the first and none of the rest. Five artefacts went that
way in two days. **This closes the CLASS rather than the five instances** — the instances were
already repaired, and repairing instances is what leaves the next one to be found by the person it
inconveniences.

**It is the freshness check's shape, one step earlier.** Every guard here watched content moving
BETWEEN stores; none watched the folder the movement passes through. A guard on what changes inside
a directory does not see a file that simply appears in it.

**Four findings; two fail.**

| finding | fails | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `BYPASS` | **yes** | staged after the door began writing sidecars, and has none — a `cp` |
| `OVERWRITTEN` | **yes** | sidecar present, bytes no longer match it — a `cp` ONTO a real delivery |
| `PRE-MECHANISM` | no | staged before sidecars existed; legitimately has none |
| `ORPHAN SIDECAR` | no | a digest whose file is gone, usually a supersede |

**`OVERWRITTEN` is the worst of the four and the one a sidecar-existence check alone would miss:**
the sidecar still LOOKS like proof, so the other store compares its bytes against a digest for
content nobody holds any more. **A stale receipt is worse than no receipt.**

**THE CUTOFF IS DERIVED, NOT CHOSEN.** `SIDECARS_SINCE` is the instant `deliver()` began writing
sidecars — commit `7dffe51`, 2026-08-19 23:59:07 +0100, found with `git log -S`. A hand-picked date
would be a guess about where the backlog stops; this is the fact itself. It carries its OFFSET, so
the comparison against a filesystem mtime is between two absolute instants (R80) — the session runs
BST, and a bare local date would misfile every artefact staged in the last hour of 19 August.

**Current state: 308 staged, 18 with digests, 290 PRE-MECHANISM, 0 bypassed.** The 290 are printed
by date on every run so a dated backlog cannot decay into a green tick (R61); none of them can be
verified as arrived in either direction.

**WHAT IT CANNOT SCREEN, STATED** (R60, R94): a `cp` accompanied by a hand-written matching sidecar
passes. That is not an accidental bypass, it is a forgery, and no check on this side can tell it
from a delivery. **This catches the mechanism being SKIPPED, not the mechanism being FAKED**, and a
guard that hides its bound is worse than none.

Fault-injected on all three live classes: a `cp` straight in, a `cp` onto a real delivery, and a
file removed from under its sidecar. All three reported by name.

## R344 — The tool's own word is the value; anything stronger is a claim the sending side cannot make

**David's ruling, 2026-08-20, beside R255.** `deliver()` prints `STAGED`. I wrote **"Delivered"** and
**"sent"**.

**R255 was already in force and was overridden by prose.** That is the whole finding. The rule that
only the receiving store can report arrival did not fail — it was correctly implemented, correctly
printed, and then restated one line later in a stronger word that no mechanism screens. **The gap is
not between the rule and the code; it is between the code's output and my summary of it**, and R178
already named prose as the only artefact here with no gate on it.

**The rule: when a tool states the status of an act, that word is the VALUE (R25). Report it, do not
paraphrase it upward.** `STAGED` does not become `delivered` because the copy succeeded, a
`PROPOSED` row does not become `approved` because it looks right, and a `PROVISIONAL` key does not
become `authored` because the reviewer named it. **Every one of those is a promotion by summary, and
the summary is where the promotion is invisible** — the field still says the true thing.

**Why it recurs:** the stronger word is the one that describes what you MEANT to do. Writing
"delivered" after a successful copy is not carelessness about the fact, it is accuracy about the
intention — which is exactly why it does not feel like an error while it is being written. R203's
boundary is the same shape from the other side: where a value carries doubt, a bare name asserts the
thing the doubt denies.

**No mechanism is proposed for this one, and that is deliberate.** `check:authority-shape` screens
the store and states that it cannot screen prose; nothing has changed about that. This is a written
rule for a channel with no gate, which is what the register is for.

## R345 — No readability formula. If one is ever built, it measures DECODING, is called decoding, and is never printed as a reading age

**Annie's ruling, 2026-08-20, with two passages as her evidence. Applies to every district and to
every future instrument.**

**Her evidence, in her terms.** `stream-a-03-wind-in-willows` reads **eleven to thirteen**: long
stacked sentences, words a Year 6 will not hold. The **commissioned** passage has short sentences
and plain words, so **every formula will call it easy — and it is not**. Decoding **nine or ten**;
comprehension **twelve or more**, because almost everything that matters is implied.

**The general shape: a formula measures DECODING. The §6 band is about COMPREHENSION. They come
apart hardest on exactly the modern commissioned prose this product writes for itself.** Sentence
length and syllable counts are the inputs every readability formula has; inference load is an input
none of them has. Commissioned prose is written short and plain ON PURPOSE and carries its meaning
underneath, so the formula reads the surface it was designed to read and gets the wrong answer in
the one place we most need the right one.

**The instruction if an instrument is ever built:** build it for **decoding**, **call it decoding**,
and **never print it as a reading age**. *"The day it is, that passage ships labelled easier than a
passage a child can actually read."*

**This is a naming rule with a serving consequence, not a modelling preference.** A number beside a
passage becomes that passage's reading age whatever the column heading says — the heading is read
once and the number is read every time. **The failure is not a wrong estimate; it is a right
estimate of the wrong quantity, wearing the name of the quantity somebody needed.** That is R80's
shape in an instrument nobody has built yet, and this ruling exists to stop it being built.

**IMPLEMENTED, NOT MERELY RECORDED.** The fifteen-passage pack carries **no readability figure
anywhere** and says so in its own text. The commissioning `band` is shown per passage and labelled
as what it is — a LENGTH band with a reading-age range attached at commission, never a judgement
made by reading. **A pack that printed a number would have anchored every verdict in it**, which is
the ruling being broken by the artefact that transmits it.

**A consequence worth ruling on: the verdict shape.** Her own evidence is that one number cannot
hold both, and whichever it holds it will be read as the other. So the pack PROPOSES two fields —
`decodingAge` and `comprehensionAge`, with a `why` — and says explicitly that where the two are far
apart, **the gap is a fact about the passage worth keeping, not a discrepancy to resolve.** Proposed
from her evidence; hers to replace.

## R346 — Two flag faults recorded on the rows, unrepaired, both found by reading the flag against its text

**David, 2026-08-20.** Neither is reachable by any check here, and that is the finding as much as
the faults are: **no scanner reads a flag's REASON against a passage's PROSE.**

**`stream-a-03-wind-in-willows`, flag 1** — *"the rabbit is unhurt"*. The text says *"He was bowled
over in an instant by the impatient and contemptuous Mole"* and **never returns to him**; the Mole
goes on to chaff *"the other rabbits"*. **A fair inference is written as an observation.** It is a
reasonable reading — but the flag's verdict RESTS on it, offering "unhurt" as the reason the scene
is comic rather than cruel. An inference load-bearing for a verdict should be visible as one.

**`stream-b-01`, flag 3** — *"It is never named or used, only reached for"*. The child says
***"Don't get the spray."*** It is named, in dialogue, at the turn of the scene — the most prominent
moment in the passage. The *"or used"* half holds; the *"never named"* half is wrong on the page.
**The verdict may well survive the correction** — being named is not being used — but it is
currently resting on a reason that is not true.

**RECORDED, NOT REPAIRED, and the distinction is the ruling.** Rewriting either flag would put an
agent's words into a field that reads as a reviewer's judgement (R94) **and would erase the evidence
that the flag was written that way.** `contentFlags` is untouched on both rows — verified by hashing
the array before and after. A sibling `flagRecordFaults` carries what reading found, with
`ruledOn: null`, because nobody has decided anything (R98: UNKNOWN written as UNKNOWN, never as
absence). The write asserts the flag still contains the quoted phrase and refuses if it does not — a
fault recorded against text that has since changed is a fault about whatever is there now.

## R347 — A conditional recommendation whose condition is never met is not a kept passage; it is an unkept one that reads as kept

**David, 2026-08-20.** `pnpm report:conditional-flags`. **9 of 61 flags carry a directive**, across
7 passages.

**A flag saying "keep" is a verdict. A flag saying "keep, AND do not let any question ask pupils to
state the reason" is a verdict PLUS a mitigation** — and the mitigation is the half that has to
reach an author. **This population is a different thing from the population of flags**, and it is
the one where a verdict shipped and its condition did not.

**The instance is the most reachable passage in the store.** `stream-a-03-wind-in-willows` sits
behind **22 LIVE items** and its flag ends *"a teacher note could point out that the Mole is being
cheeky, not admirable."* **No teacher note exists.** The condition was never met and nothing
noticed, **because no field holds it and no code reads it** — the condition exists only inside the
sentence that states the verdict, so a reader who acts on the verdict has already read past it.

**Reported, not gated.** The standard these flags are judged against does not exist, and a gate
would enforce a rule nobody has written.

**Its bound, stated** (R60): recommendations are PROSE, so conditionality is found by keyword —
directive words that tell a later reader to do or not do something. That over-calls and under-calls.
**9 is a floor, not a census.** And **the correct repair is not a better pattern**: it is a
recommendation being a FIELD with a condition slot and a met/unmet state rather than a sentence.
That is a governance decision and nothing here takes it.

## R348 — Normalise a field path to its container BEFORE the set arrives, not after it reports total disagreement

**2026-08-20.** Cowork's declaration set is announced as **97 spans, 89 items, 29 banks, with
per-span digests and DOTTED FIELD PATHS** (`stem.text`, `explanation.walkScript`). Ours keys on the
CONTAINER (`stem`, `explanation`). **Both name the same thing at different depths.**

**Left unnormalised, `check:declaration-sets` would have reported 314 divergences on first contact —
every one of their 97 absent from ours and all 157 of ours absent from theirs** — and the headline
would have been total disagreement between two stores that may largely agree. **A reader that
cannot parse, reporting a fact about the content** (R173), on the check's first real run, about the
very thing it was built to measure.

**The fix is one line and the timing is the entry.** The shape was ANNOUNCED before the set arrived,
and the announcement is a thing you can act on — a mismatch found by reading a description costs a
regex, and the same mismatch found by running the check costs an investigation into 314 phantom
divergences and a message to the other store about a disagreement that does not exist. Fault-tested
by re-expressing all 157 of our own spans in the announced shape: **0 divergences, where the
unnormalised reader gave 314.**

## R349 — THE CLASS: nothing reads a judgement's REASON against the text it judges

**David, 2026-08-20, generalising from R346's two faults. Recorded because this is the gap the
standard will have to say something about.**

**Both faults were found by a person reading the flag against the passage. Neither is reachable by
any instrument on either side, and no instrument is proposed here** — because naming the class
honestly is the prerequisite for anyone deciding whether one is possible.

**What every check here actually screens.** The scanners read child-facing STRINGS for banned
vocabulary, reading age, notation, id leaks. `check:line-refs` compares a citation to a passage.
`check:source-quotes` compares a declared span to its source. `check:authority-shape` reads the
store's attribution columns. **Every one of them compares a value to a rule, or a value to another
value. Not one of them compares a CLAIM to the TEXT IT IS A CLAIM ABOUT.**

**So a whole class of judgement is unscreened, and it is the class that carries the most weight per
sentence:**

- a flag's `reason` — *"the rabbit is unhurt"*, when the text bowls him over and never returns
- a flag's `element` — a description of what is in a passage
- a `curationNote`, an `editorialNote`, a `why` on a band
- a misconception's `description` against the items tagged with it
- a walk script's account of a line against that line

**These are all PROSE ABOUT A TEXT, and they are all checked the same way: by someone reading both.**
That is not a gap in coverage, it is a gap in KIND — no amount of extending the existing scanners
reaches it, because they are string-shaped and this is comparison-shaped.

**Why it is the dangerous class.** A wrong string fails a gate. **A wrong claim about a text passes
every gate and then becomes the reason for a verdict.** In both instances the faulty clause was
load-bearing: *"the rabbit is unhurt"* is offered as the reason the scene is comic rather than cruel,
and *"never named"* is offered as the reason the insecticide is acceptable. **The verdict survives
in the store while the reason for it is false, and nothing anywhere records the discrepancy.**

**The R173 connection, which is why this is worth a number.** R173 said a disagreeing number gets
investigated for free and a confirming one has to be investigated on purpose. **This class is the
same asymmetry in prose**: a flag whose reason sounds right is never checked against the text,
because it sounds right. Both of these read perfectly well until someone opened the passage.

**Recorded, not repaired, with `ruledOn: null` on both rows** — nobody has decided whether either
verdict survives its correction, and that is a reviewer's call, not a repair.

**What the standard has to say something about**, stated as the open question rather than answered:
when a flag's reason makes a factual claim about the passage, **is that claim part of the judgement
(so correcting it reopens the verdict) or part of the explanation (so correcting it does not)?**
R346's two cases point opposite ways — the rabbit claim looks load-bearing and the naming claim
looks recoverable — and nothing currently distinguishes them.

## R350 — The pack is not called a reading-age pack, and the two columns may never be printed as one

**Annie's ruling extended by David, 2026-08-20, following R345.**

**Neither `decodingAge` nor `comprehensionAge` is a reading age, and neither may be printed as one** —
not in an export, not in a staff view, not in a parent view, and **not as a fallback when only one
number is available. If only one of the two can be shown, none is shown.** A lone number in either
column is the single-number failure R345 is about, arriving through the door marked *"we only had
room for one"*, which is the door it will actually arrive through.

**The pack was requested as a reading-age pack and is not called one.** The title was changed to
*"for decoding and comprehension verdicts"*, because **a pack titled by the quantity the ruling says
does not exist writes every verdict inside it toward that quantity.** The request keeps its name in
conversation; the artefact takes the name of what it actually asks for. The filename changed with
it — a name that does not identify its payload is R88's fault in a title.

**The two-number shape goes as a PROPOSAL and it is hers to replace or ratify.** It is derived from
her own evidence — decoding nine or ten against comprehension twelve or more, on one passage — and
derivation from evidence is not the same as a decision. **Where the two numbers are far apart, the
gap is a fact about the passage worth keeping, not a discrepancy to resolve.**

## R351 — The join compares containers, and says so whenever that loses information

**David's question, 2026-08-20, asked and settled BEFORE the first join rather than after it
reported.**

**Both stores emit depth 1**: ours **by construction** — `field` comes from a literal two-element
loop and cannot be deeper without a code change — and Cowork's **by observation** across its 97 rows.
So the choice was being made on data that does not exercise it, which is the only condition under
which it can be made calmly.

**Joining on the FULL PATH is wrong**: our side cannot emit one, so any deeper path the other store
ever sends is unmatched — R348's 314-divergence failure, one level down.

**Joining on the CONTAINER is right today and carries the inverse risk**: `stem.text` and
`stem.prompt` collapse to one key, so a span declared against a different sub-field reads as the same
field. **That converts a class-1 or class-2 divergence into class 3, or into agreement — and class 3
is what the whole check exists to catch.**

**So: normalise for the join, carry `fieldPath` UNNORMALISED on every row, and report the moment
either side emits depth > 1** — naming the affected rows and saying plainly that their divergence
counts are not trustworthy until the join key is ruled on. **A normalisation nobody can see is
indistinguishable from data that never needed it**, and the run now states which of the two it is
looking at every time.

## R352 — A derived shape block: the emission states its own structure, computed by the walk that produced the rows

**Cowork's proposal, adopted on both sides, 2026-08-20.**

**A shape computed FROM the rows cannot drift from the rows.** An announcement in a message can: it
is written once, by hand, about data that changes afterwards, and it is known only to whoever read
that message. **The shape block survives a reader who never saw the announcement — which is every
future reader.**

Nothing in it is hand-listed: key names come from the rows' own keys, the depth histogram and the
distinct paths from the values. It carries `rowCount`, `rowKeys`, `distinctItems`, `fieldPathDepths`,
`distinctFieldPaths`, the `joinKey` and its stated caveat.

**And the check reads shape BEFORE rows.** If two emissions disagree about their own structure,
every row-level number is a consequence of that disagreement rather than a finding about content —
**reporting divergences first presents a structural mismatch as a content dispute, which is the most
expensive way for two stores to argue.** Cowork's first set carries no shape block; that is reported
as a fact about the artefact, not a failure.

## R353 — The join ran: 95 of 97 agree, the disagreement is one-directional, and every apparent conflict was manufactured by the display

**2026-08-20. Cowork's set arrived mid-run and the reader REFUSED it** — its rows sit at `spans`, not
`declarations`, and `readCoworkSet` threw naming the eight top-level keys it found instead of
returning empty. **That refusal is why the first join was correct rather than reporting 97 phantom
absences** (R173 working as designed). `spans` was then ADDED to the recognised row keys, after being
seen — never guessed.

**The result: 64 divergences of 157 vs 97, and not one of them is a contradiction.**

| class | count |
|---|---:|
| field declared here, not there at all | 56 |
| field declared there, not here at all | **2** |
| same field, an extra span held here only | 6 |
| same field, an extra span held there only | 0 |

**95 of their 97 spans match ours exactly.** The two that do not are both on `ENG-019-BV-02` — **an
item this store does not hold at all** (we have `ENG-019-BV-09` through `-12`). **The declaration
comparison found a missing ITEM, which is not what it was built to look for.**

**EVERY APPARENT CONFLICT WAS THE DISPLAY, AND CATCHING THAT COST ONE QUERY.** The six class-3 rows
rendered as *we declare "trotted as one trots…" / they declare "exciting stories"* — two stores
disagreeing about one span. **They are not: both spans are ours, on a field where they hold one and
we hold two.** In all six, their span is present in our set. The report now prints the other side's
span **only when we genuinely do not hold it**, and the class is renamed to *an extra span held here
only*. **A manufactured conflict, in the class the check exists to catch, is worse than no report.**

**A hypothesis of mine was refuted by the data and is recorded because the refutation is the useful
part.** Seeing `"stupid"` and `"contemptuous"` against our full quotations, I proposed that the two
stores declare different THINGS — they the exempted word, we the citation. **The counts refute it:
48 of their 97 are single words and 47 of our 157 are, and 47 of those 48 match exactly.** The
populations are the same kind; ours is simply larger.

**And their `againstCode` note reconciles.** Cowork records that *"a figure of 113 was relayed and is
NOT reconciled"*. **113 was our distinct-ITEM count; 97 is their SPAN count — different units, not
disagreeing measurements.** The comparable pairs are **157 spans against 97**, and **113 items
against 89**. Nothing was wrong on either side; a number crossed without its unit attached, which is
R203's shape in a relayed figure.

## R354 — The join's first run is CONFIRMED-BY-INSPECTION, not CARRIED

**Cowork's caveat, 2026-08-20, and it applies to this register as much as to its own.**

R351 settled the join key on the finding that **both sides emit depth 1**. That finding is true and
**it is not vouched for by either artefact.** Ours was read from an emission that PREDATES the shape
block, plus a read of the emitter source (`ourDeclarationSet` builds `field` from a literal
two-element loop). Theirs was read by counting 97 rows in a file that carries no shape block at all.
**Both are inspections. Neither is a declaration.**

**The distinction is the same one this register keeps making about arrival** (R255) **and about
prose overriding a rule** (R344): *a fact established by looking is not a fact the artefact states.*
An inspection is valid on the day it is made, by the person who made it, about the bytes in front of
them. It does not travel, it does not survive the next emission, and **nothing re-checks it.**

So the status is recorded as **CONFIRMED-BY-INSPECTION**, and the upgrade condition is written down:
**only the NEXT emission from each side gets to say its shape is in the file.** Ours now carries the
derived block (R352) and will qualify on its next run; Cowork's qualifies when it adopts one.

**Recording it this way costs nothing today and is the only thing that will be legible in a month**,
when the depth-1 claim is load-bearing for a join key nobody remembers choosing.

## R355 — The item populations differ by FIVE, and all five are the same known event nothing was watching

**David, 2026-08-20.** `pnpm check:item-population`. Asked because `check:declaration-sets` found
`ENG-019-BV-02` **by accident** — it compares declarations, and that item happened to carry two.

**It is not the only one. There are five**, each named in Cowork artefacts with no row in this store:

| item | siblings here |
|---|---|
| `ENG-018-RB-01` | RB-02 … RB-12 present, this one absent |
| `ENG-018-RB-11` | same family, same shape |
| `ENG-019-BV-02` | BV-01 … BV-12 present, this one absent |
| `ENG-023-RT-08` | RT-01 … RT-12 present, this one absent |
| `ENG-027-RR-08` | RR-01 … RR-12 present, this one absent |

**Every one is a single missing member of a family otherwise complete here** — which is what a
failed per-item import looks like, and nothing like drift.

**AND THEY RECONCILE EXACTLY TO A KNOWN BACKLOG.** `REISSUESIXITEMS.json` names six items reissued
after they were found never to have crossed. **`ENG-015-CC-12` landed on 2026-08-19 after the
ban-list fix. The other five never did**, and the reissue file has sat in the inbound folder since,
its own header stating *"zero ids exist only on Code's side, so this is a one-directional loss."*

**So the finding is not five mystery items. It is that a reissue nobody was watching land did not
land, and the only thing that noticed was a check built for something else.** Every guard here
watches content ARRIVING correctly; **none watched whether a named, staged, agreed reissue actually
completed.** That is R88's return leg pointing inward — an untravelled path and an absent path are
the same thing, and this one was travelled halfway.

**THE BOUND, STATED, BECAUSE IT IS MOST OF THE CHECK'S HONESTY.** It compares our item table against
every item id appearing in any Cowork artefact we hold. **That is not Cowork's item population.** An
item Cowork holds that appears in none of the artefacts it has sent is invisible here and always will
be — **only Cowork can report Cowork's population**, exactly as only the receiving store can report
arrival. So the two directions are labelled differently and only one is a finding:
`THEIRS_NOT_OURS` is real (they named it, so it exists there); **`OURS_NOT_MENTIONED` is 270 and is
printed as a COUNT, never as a finding**, because it measures the instrument and not the content.

The id pattern is DERIVED from our own 1033 ids (R57) — every distinct id shape becomes a matcher, so
a family added tomorrow is scanned tomorrow rather than falling silently outside a hand-written list.

## R356 — An artefact that describes an act is not the act

**David, 2026-08-20.** `pnpm check:reissue-completion`.

**Every guard here watches whether content ARRIVES CORRECTLY** — import gates, per-item digests,
outbound sidecars, declaration sets, the staging queue. **None watched whether a described act
COMPLETED.** `REISSUESIXITEMS.json` named six items on 19 August. One landed. Five did not. The
artefact sat in the inbound folder for a month asserting they had been sent, and **the only thing
that noticed was `check:item-population` — a check built for a different question, which found one
of the five by accident because it happened to carry two declarations.**

**The class is wider than reissues: migrations, retag lists, ratify-and-write acts — anything whose
whole content is a promise that N things will be true afterwards.** A file that says *"these six are
reissued"* is evidence of an intention, not of a state, and nothing in this repo has ever read one
as a claim to be checked.

**EVERY ID CARRIES A DISPOSITION, AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES THE CHECK SURVIVABLE.**

| disposition | meaning |
|---|---|
| `IMPORTED` | the id is in the item table; the act completed for this id |
| `REFUSED` | absent, AND a ledger entry records why, with a date and who can repair it |
| `UNDISPOSED` | absent, and **nothing says why** — the only failure |

**A reissue can legitimately not complete**, and `ENG-019-BV-02` is that case: held at the door for a
fault only Cowork can repair. **Without the REFUSED state, one correctly-held item would keep this
check permanently red, and it would be muted inside a week** — the failure mode already named twice
on this board (`check:staging-queue`, `check:declaration-sets`). **UNDISPOSED is exactly the state
the five were in**: not imported, not refused, not recorded, with an artefact on disk asserting
otherwise.

The refusal reasons are written **from the gate's own output**, never typed by hand (R25), and the

both an item id and an item body, so a delivery is checked and a report is not — never by filename.

## R358 — A superseded value stored inside the field it supersedes is read as live

**David, 2026-08-21, relaying Cowork's finding — the same fault present on both sides.**

`_previousText` sits inside `stem` beside `text`. `_previousWalkScript` sits inside `explanation`
beside `walkScript`. **Anything walking the container reads the superseded value as live, and the
child-facing gate walks exactly those containers.** A reword that successfully removed a banned word
would keep failing on the copy of the pre-reword text kept beside it — **and the failure would read
as a live content defect**, which is how it manufactured a cross-store divergence that did not exist.

**36 items, six shapes**: `stem._previousText` (26, beside live `text`), `stem._previousQuotes` (4),
`explanation._previousHintCore` (7 + 4), `explanation._previousWalkScript` (3, all **LIVE**),
`stem._previousText2` (3).

**ZERO BLOCKING FAILURES ARE RAISED ON ONE TODAY, AND THAT IS AN OUTCOME, NOT EVIDENCE THE DESIGN
HELD** (R62). Baselined before and after the repair: **nothing moved, 0 newly pass, 0 newly fail.**
The coupling is live, unguarded, and simply has not been exercised — which is exactly the state
`distractors.ts` was in when R62 was written.

**The gate now refuses to read them** (`isSuperseded` in `item-content-gate.ts`, skipping any path
segment beginning `_`). **That is a READER-SIDE SKIP AND NOT A REPAIR**: the next reader written
against `stem` walks them again. `pnpm check:superseded-inside-field` reports the 36 as the
population to move, and the right shape is Cowork's — stamps OUTSIDE the container, in a
`_superseded` sibling of the field rather than inside it. Reported and not failed, because these are
real history and moving them is a migration with reviewed content on the other side.

## R359 — The join key stays CONTAINER-ONLY, because an index is not an identity

**David, 2026-08-21, reopening R351 on new data.** Cowork's current emission is **97 rows, 96 at
depth 1 and one at depth 2** — `ENG-018-RB-01` field `options[2]`, the `favoring` declaration.

**Ruling: container-only. Not full path, and not full path with index normalisation.**

**An index is not stable across a reorder**, and option order is a thing this product deliberately
changes — `pinVerdictOptionsLast` reorders options at serve time, and a shuffle is seeded per
occasion. So a class-three comparison keyed on `options[2]` would report a divergence **caused by
option ordering**, in the class that exists to catch two stores disagreeing about the same span.
That is a manufactured conflict, which R353 has already recorded once this week.

**Index normalisation (`options[2]` → `options[]`) is better and still wrong here**, for a reason
that is specific rather than general: **it buys sub-field precision this store cannot use.** Our
option content carries exactly two keys across all 3820 options — `value` and `label` — and **zero
options carry a `quotes` array**. There is nothing at option level for a finer key to distinguish,
so the precision would be bought entirely on credit against a shape that does not exist (R61).

**Revisit when option-level declarations have a storage shape here.** At that point index
normalisation becomes the right key, and this entry is the record of why it was not chosen earlier.

## R361 — Call the gate, never rebuild it: enforceable here, and scoped

**David, 2026-08-21.** Registered on Cowork's side as DECLARED rather than enforced, deliberately,
since nothing there can assert a claim about this store. **Here it is enforceable, and R357 is the
case for it** — a hand-built gate call held five items for twelve faults that were not there.

**The check cannot be written usefully today, and the reason is the design, not the effort.** There
is no shared builder to assert against: `import-english-items.ts` constructs its `optionRows` inline,
and every other caller does the same. A check asserting *"nobody constructs a gate input by hand"*
would fail every existing call site, including the governing one.

**So the order is: extract `gateInputFromItem()` into `packages/core` first, migrate the call sites
to it, THEN assert that every `checkItemChildFacing` call passes its output.** That final assertion
is cheap and static — a scan for the call, checking its argument is the builder's result. Scoped and
not built, with the sequence recorded so it is not attempted in the wrong order.

## R362 — Control-class audit: three assert the instrument FIRES, one asserts it stays silent

**David, 2026-08-21.** Quiet controls read empty input as a pass; flipping controls invert on a clean
store. **Audited all four named controls for which kind each is.**

| control | input | asserts | kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| `check-card-gives-key` `CONTROLS` | literal `[key, text]` pairs | the variant matcher **fires** | fixture, catches blindness |
| `check-no-review-furniture` `CONTROL_SAMPLE` | literal string | the furniture detector **fires** | fixture, catches blindness |
| `check-pilot-review-excluded` `CANARY` | a synthetic file it creates | the exclusion **fires** | fixture, catches blindness |
| `audit-declarations` control probe | literal `GOOD_QUOTE` | the gate raises **NOTHING** | fixture, **QUIET** |

**No control asserts a fault's presence in the LIVE STORE**, which is the flipping kind and the one
that inverts the day the store is cleaned. All four run against fixtures, so none can be broken by
repairing content — that is what the earlier conversion from live instances bought.

**But the fourth cannot catch a blind instrument, and that is worth stating rather than counting it
as a fourth control.** `audit-declarations`'s control passes when a well-formed declaration produces
no failure. **If the gate stopped firing entirely, that control would still report `CONTROL OK`** —
it is R60's question 2 answered in the negative. A clean-input control proves the instrument is not
over-firing; only a planted-fault control proves it is working at all. **The audit needs one of
each, and it has one.**

## R365 — The prose number is derived, and fixing it exposed a stamp that did not cover its own file

**David, 2026-08-21.** `recognition-test-for-annie` said *"The 20 already held for a string match come
first"* while `denominators`, three lines below in the same object, **derived** the same quantity and
got **19**. The data was self-consistent (19 held + 21 remaining = 40); **only the sentence
disagreed**, and it was going to the reviewer as a description of the order she was about to read in.

**IT WAS NOT CORRECTED TO 19.** The sentence now derives its number from the rows, like the
denominator beside it. **Typing 19 would rot again the next time the card-hold set moves**, silently,
exactly as 20 rotted — R180's finding, in an object that was already computing the right answer one
field away. **A number in prose describing our own data is derived or declared, never both typed and
computed in the same payload.**

**AND THE FIX EXPOSED A LARGER FAULT THAN THE ONE IT REPAIRED.** The stamp was computed over `rows`
alone (`stampedOver: ['rows']`) while the file delivers `what`, `herStandard`,
`whyThisIsStagedAndNotJudged`, `readingOrder`, `denominators` **and** `rows`. **So the prose change
altered the payload and would NOT have moved the stamp or the stamped filename — two materially
different files under one name**, which is precisely the fault R88 recorded against the misconception
library. **It was live here and invisible because nothing had yet edited the prose without touching a
row.**

The stamp now covers every field the file delivers; `8399589fc16b8189` became `b8c8e3ccad8ddf8f`, and
`deliver()` removed the superseded file and its sidecar rather than leaving them alongside. **Nothing
in the 40 rows changed** — same items, same order, flagged cases still first.

**The general rule: `stampedOver` is the file's whole payload, or the name is a claim about part of
it.** A projection narrower than the delivery is a name that cannot detect a change to what was
delivered.

## R368 — The conditional-recommendation schema: four decisions, and the two-verdict split that dissolved the expensive question

**Annie's ruling, 2026-08-21.** `packages/core/src/conditional-recommendation.ts`.

**Three agreed as proposed.** `KEEP_IF` is its own verdict — *"the mitigation sits exactly where a
reader stops reading; a separate word is the whole mechanism and a boolean beside KEEP would be
skippable in the way prose is."* `UNMET` is the written default — *"the empty-array problem in a new
field, and an unmet condition and an unexamined one must not share a representation."* `WAIVED`
requires a reason — *"a waiver without one is a silent keep with extra steps."*

**HER ADDITION, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MAKES THE OTHER THREE WORK: the condition names who can meet
it.** *"A teacher note points out that the Mole is being cheeky"* has no owner, and **an obligation
with nobody to meet it is UNMET BY CONSTRUCTION FOREVER.** `owner` is required and a condition
proposed without one is **refused at authoring** — *"otherwise the backlog is guaranteed rather than
possible."* Enforced in `refuseFlagAtAuthoring`, at the only point where the person who knows the
answer is present.

**THE TWO-VERDICT SPLIT DISSOLVED THE EXPENSIVE QUESTION RATHER THAN COMPROMISING ON IT.** The
proposed `kind` enum classified by where the obligation LANDS — useful for routing, and it *"does not
answer the question that matters, which is whether the passage is acceptable without the condition."*

- **`KEEP_IF`** — the condition IMPROVES a passage that is already acceptable.
- **`RETIRE_UNLESS`** — the passage is NOT acceptable without it.
- **Serving blocks on `RETIRE_UNLESS` only** — *"the honest version of the position that makes
  conditions load-bearing, applied only where they are."*
- **Publishing blocks on both**, so the population stops growing.

**`stream-a-03-wind-in-willows` is ruled `KEEP_IF` and its 22 LIVE items keep serving.** *"A child
reading the Mole being rude and jeering does not need a note to survive it, and Grahame's own
narration already calls him impatient and contemptuous. The note improves the passage; it is not what
makes it acceptable."* **The expensive case was settled by ruling on the passage rather than by
choosing a policy compromise, which is the right order** — I had costed three positions and
recommended the middle one, and she moved the question instead of answering it.

**HER RIDER: each existing UNMET condition takes a date** on which it is met, waived with a reason,
or **the verdict reopens** — *"a backlog with no date is the thing everyone learns to ignore."*
`reviewBy` is required and `verdictReopens()` is a state change, not a warning.

**AND HER OWN RULE BLOCKS APPLYING HER OWN RULING, WHICH IS THE MECHANISM WORKING.** Wind in the
Willows cannot be re-expressed as a structured `KEEP_IF` today: `owner` and `reviewBy` are required,
she has ruled the verdict and not named either, and `refuseFlagAtAuthoring` refuses it. **Inventing an
owner to make the ruling applicable is exactly the fault the field exists to prevent.** The nine
re-express when she supplies owners and dates; the machine converts none of them (R347).
