`ENG-001-WIW-19` shows the format working on sight: *"Went without any food"* on *made fast* is a
sense of a DIFFERENT PARSE — *fast* the noun, not *made fast* the verb phrase — which is exactly the

## R616 — The standing path cannot carry an approve-as-written, and the exposure list follows

**David's two questions, answered from the code rather than from the week's behaviour.**

**ONE: the write site.** The standing path that sets `hintAuthoredBy`/`hintAuthority` on an item is
`apply-all-unlanded.ts:177-185`, fed only by amendments the shared reader extracts. **It is NOT
reachable from a ruling that changes no text**: line 170 — `if (before === h.authored) { ALREADY;
continue; }` — skips the whole write, authorship included. The guard is right about idempotence and
wrong about rulings: **it conflates "nothing to write" with "nothing ruled".** An
approved-as-written verdict has travelled only through hand-written one-shots
(`apply-annie-27th-hints.ts:70`, verdict `APPROVED`), never through the standing path. **"Approved

## R618 — The non-ACTIVE entries carry nothing; the resolver's status filter is PROPOSED, not written

**Count first: `en-error-spot-false-positive` (REJECTED) and `en-vocab-secondary-sense` (RETIRED)
have ZERO carriers.** No option anywhere holds either tag, so no rejected or retired wording is
reachable by a child today and nothing takes an R498 flag. The hole in the resolver is real and
currently empty.

**THE DESIGN (no write until ruled):**

- **The resolver returns the library hint only from an ACTIVE entry.** A tag resolving to a
  non-ACTIVE entry serves as if the option were UNTAGGED — the child gets nothing rather than a
  wording a reviewer rejected. **The fallthrough is named: `undefined`, the same value an untagged
  option already produces**, chosen because it is the one state every caller already handles.
- **It cannot fall through silently.** The resolver's choice type grows a reason —
  `why: 'tag resolves to a RETIRED/REJECTED entry'` — so serving-nothing-by-status is
  distinguishable from serving-nothing-by-untagged in any transcript or log, and R601's fault (two
  states, one output) is not rebuilt into the fix.
- **The check with no input:** `check:non-active-carriers` — every option whose tag resolves
  non-ACTIVE. Its population CAN legitimately be empty (it is today), so it calls
  `declareMayBeEmpty` with the reason printed on every run, and asserts the SCREENED denominator
  (options with tags) non-empty — the R582 shape, so a broken query cannot read as a clean bank.

**The 66 was never printed.** A composed number was re-described downstream as a computed one, and

evidence.**

the derivation, and a figure with neither carries no verb at all.*

**The rule, minted on the cache repair the desk endorsed (David, 2026-08-24, beside R674's
landing): a denormalised column is a CACHE of provenance, aligned by TRANSCRIPTION, never a
second judgement.** The instance: the seven transported rows held her approval in
`textProvenance` and in AMENDED events on rev-0001, while the `approvedBy` column read null — the
record and its cache disagreed, and the repair copied the record into the cache. What the rule
forbids is the tempting extra step: minting an APPROVED event to "complete" the repair would have
been a machine verdict wearing her name (R94) — the alignment writes only what the record already
holds, and adds no act to the history. The test for which side is the record: the one carrying
the authority citation and the date; the cache is whichever copy exists for readers' convenience.

the class-closure declaration on `annie-125-nine-landing-51c3d4e7e035f878.json` stands as the

**Ruled (Annie's 156th thread, David, 2026-08-25): underscore-prefixed before-images are

destroys the record it exists to hold. Cowork's screen found six punctuation faults in

retained before-image is a record of what was repaired"*. Implemented as `isRetentionPath`, and

on the day it appears. `stem._previousText` reclassified accordingly.

## R716 — A question type's own orthography is not emphasis

**Ruled: the shouted-capitals rule binds EMPHASIS ONLY.** vr-06 renders the target `SHOUT`, the
frame `SH___` and the option `OUT` in capitals BECAUSE the child is completing letters; a
joins-with prompt capitalises `AIR` because it is the thing being joined. **Probed before the
rule was written — all four pass the item gate clean — so this changes no verdict**; it is a
named constant that stops a LATER gate flagging orthography without meeting the ruling. Cowork's
450 notation hits would have been 450 wrong verdicts, and it NAMED them rather than scoring them:
the qualifier lesson in a third guise, caught by the store that would have been marked down by it.

its own `DISPOSITIONS` map and its own `isScreened` predicate — `walked && text.includes(' ')` —
a RE-DERIVATION of the gate rather than a call to it, **wrong in both directions**: it reported
single-token option values as unscreened when the gate screens them, and it could not see the
gate walking `explanation` through a three-name list. **That predicate produced the 1,533 figure
that sent a correct ruling after the wrong hole.** Both are deleted. One membership
(`FIELD_DISPOSITIONS`), one function (`dispositionFor`/`isScreenedPath`), no second
implementation. **The check's own header had already written the remedy** — *a verifier states
its source before it runs, and calls the family's own function rather than re-deriving the
property* — and this is that rule applied to the file that wrote it.

**Result: the check now walks the whole row and reports CHILD 0 UNSCREENED.** It also surfaces

## R719 — The notation exemption has a boundary: a capital in a stem cannot claim it

**Her scope line, taken as the whole rule**: *notation is exempt where the string is an IDENTIFIER
OR SYMBOL IN ITS OWN SYSTEM, and never where it sits inside a sentence a child reads. A code
letter in a series is notation; a capital inside a stem is emphasis wearing notation's coat.*

Wired as `notationExempt(root, path, text)`, which requires **both** conditions and neither alone:
the PATH must be one that carries symbols (`NOTATION_BEARING_PATHS`), **and the STRING must BE a
symbol** — one token, no sentence punctuation. `stem.prompt` fails the first. **A capital inside
any sentence fails the second on every path, including the notation-bearing ones**, because
`options[].content.value` is a single letter on a VR card and a full sentence on a comprehension
one — the same field name carrying two kinds of content, which is the trap this boundary exists
for. Four tests, including the one that matters: *"Which word joins with AIR…"* is refused the
exemption while a bare `AIR` keeps it.

**And the thirty cleared**: all thirty undeclared paths ruled STAFF — sixteen
`draftSelfAssessment.*`, three `stem.quotes[].*`, two `stemRedraft.*`, nine singletons. Re-run:
**staff 62 · child 0 · quotation 2 · undecided 0 · UNDECLARED 0**, and the gate over 335 LIVE
items reports **0 failing, zero content faults**.

## R721 — A known member drawn from the standing corpus expires when the corpus is repaired

**Cowork's lesson, taken whole and audited against my own instruments.** Its bank screen wired its
known member to the shouted TWO — a fault in the STANDING CORPUS — and **the moment the 28 rows
were amended the screen refused, because the member it was built knowing about had been
repaired**. Its sentence, which is the rule: *a screen whose self-test expires goes dark exactly
when the corpus is at its cleanest — the moment it is least likely to be questioned.*

**The audit** (`fixture-audit-5dbe34a6cabef6f6.json`, file sha256
`5dbe34a6cabef6f65640c9c750f8fd65fdeda5ebabbd2c836d72ce10cd1e3f08`), limits first: it reads
SOURCE, not behaviour, and covers `scripts/check-*.ts` only. Of 80 checks: 10 already carry
synthetic/planted canaries, 4 anchor to a constant or a function name rather than to content, and
**64 have no self-test at all** — named as membership, not repaired, because a fixture is a design
decision per instrument.

**TWO CONVERTED, and the second is the sharper finding:**
- `check-content-flags` was **CORPUS-DRAWN**: its calibration specimen was the christmas-carol
  `DECLARED(item-set)` flag, a real flag in the standing corpus. **The day Annie rules that flag
  away — a legitimate content decision — the census would have gone blind while printing a clean
  run.** Now a carried fixture of four synthetic passages; the corpus specimen is still OBSERVED
  and reported, because losing the observation loses evidence — it simply no longer decides trust.
- `check-every-string-field` had **NO SELF-TEST AT ALL**, which is worse than one that expires —
  **and it is the check that produced the 1,533 figure by modelling the gate instead of calling
  it. An instrument with no self-test cannot be caught being wrong by anything but an argument,
  which is exactly what happened.**

**The shared path** is `scripts/lib/carried-fixture.ts`: `assertFixture` REFUSES a malformed
fixture (one lacking a clean case, or lacking a must-catch case — one without the other proves
half an instrument), prints **FIXTURE PASSED before the sweep** so a reader knows the instrument
worked before reading what it found, and exits non-zero when the instrument does not do what it
claims. **Every fixture carries at least one CLEAN string that must be caught by NOTHING**,
because a screen that flags clean text reports faults nobody can trust.

**Her line for the register, from the same sitting**: the reconstruction cost is **one row in
eighteen** — *"a figure where the argument used to have an opinion"*.

## R722 — Gap markers are exempt wherever they sit; the sentence is where the gap must appear

**Ruled**: a gap marker is a symbol in its own system even inside prose a child reads — **the one
string that can be, because moving it out of the sentence destroys the question.** `___(2)___` in
a cloze carrier and `SH___` in a vr-06 frame are the same object in two shapes. **The exemption is
for THE MARKER, never the sentence around it**: everything outside the marker spans is screened
exactly as before. Wired as `gapMarkerSpans` and `capitalRunIsExempt`.

## R723 — A stimulus word in a prompt is not notation; it amends to quoted form

**Ruled**: a stimulus word sits inside a sentence a child reads, so it cannot claim the
orthography exemption, and it **amends to QUOTED form under her 142nd's precedent** — the same
move that took the shouted TWO to lowercase. Landed at the generator AND on 25 derived rows:
`Which word joins with TOOTH…` → `Which word joins with "tooth"…`, the gate re-run clean on every
row, one event on the template id. Quotation marks name the word as the thing being joined
without shouting it.

**THE PROBE DAVID ASKED FOR, and it holds**: a bare shout in a stem can claim NEITHER exemption —
not on `stem.text`, not on `stem.sentence`, and not even on a notation-bearing path, because the
string is a sentence. Four tests carry it.

## R724 — The membership crosses in an importable form: one membership, both stores

**Cowork asked, and its screen re-derives child/quotation/staff by a leaf-name rule of its own.**
That is the same second-implementation fault this store removed from its own check two turns ago
(R717) — **two implementations agreeing proves only that they agree** — and this is the other half
of that repair. `field-dispositions-for-cowork-937f0bacbf89042d.json`, file sha256
`937f0bacbf89042d8e06d223b183b4a892ec4e9fb010fda70484edfda80fecd6`: 115 paths, GENERATED from the
live constants and never transcribed, because a copied membership is a second implementation
wearing a data hat.

**It carries the four things that are RULES rather than lists** — retention by underscore,
symbol-hood by shape, gap markers wherever they sit, stimulus words never — each as a named
predicate, **with eleven CONFORMANCE CASES so an importer can run its own implementation against
them and prove it agrees.** The fixture discipline (R721) applied to a crossing: a membership that
cannot be verified on arrival is prose.

## R725 — No bulk conversion: a check earns its fixture before its next emission crosses

**Ruled, and it is the better rule.** The sixty-four checks without a self-test are NOT converted
in bulk: **a check gets a carried fixture before its next emission crosses the desk** — the rate
at which they actually matter. Inventing sixty-four fixtures at once would produce sixty-four
untested assertions about instruments nobody is currently reading, which is the fault the fixture
rule exists to prevent, arriving as a tidy-up.

**The audit's membership is STANDING** (`fixture-audit-5dbe34a6cabef6f6.json`, sha256
`5dbe34a6…1e3f08`): of 80 checks, 2 now carry fixtures, 10 carry synthetic/planted canaries, 4
anchor to a constant or function name, **64 have no self-test**. The list is the queue, and the
trigger is a crossing rather than a calendar.

## R726 — Every figure from an unfixtured instrument crosses saying so, marked at the door

**Her clause and David's wiring instruction together: the mark goes INTO THE EMISSION, never into
the covering message — "a mark that depends on someone remembering to write it is the class we
just closed."** Wired in `deliver()`, the one door every artefact passes, and applied BEFORE the
bytes are copied, so **the mark is inside the file the digest is taken over and cannot be
separated from the figures it qualifies**. Whether an emitter is fixtured is read from its own
source (does it call `assertFixture`), not declared by it. It deliberately OVER-MARKS: a
membership crossing is not a check's figure, but marking it costs a reader one honest line while
missing a genuine unfixtured figure costs them a wrong belief.

**The mechanism broke a different rule on its first run, and the fix is at the door too**:
marking rewrote the file AFTER `stampedName` had hashed it, so the name claimed a content hash
the bytes no longer had — **R88's rule broken by the mechanism built to honour Annie's**. The
stamp is now RE-DERIVED from the marked bytes and the file renamed automatically, printing
`restamped →` when it happens. A name that disagrees with its own content is exactly what this
store keeps closing.

## R727 — A replacement lands before its predecessor leaves

**Cowork's migration order, ruled by David and superseding the instruction it answers**:
membership crosses → the screen rewires to import → **the rewired screen runs against its carried
fixture** → and only then does the re-derivation go. *A replacement lands before its predecessor
leaves.* **The conformance cases are what make that provable, which is why they matter more than
the paths** — without them the middle step is a claim.

**Owned in the same entry: my own R717 repair did not follow this order.** I deleted
`check:every-string-field`'s `DISPOSITIONS` map and its `isScreened` predicate in the same edit
that added the import, and verified afterwards. It happened to work; the order says it should
have been provable before the old path went. The rule is registered against my own precedent, not
only against Cowork's plan.

## R728 — The membership re-crosses; a digest is inline only where it CAN be

**The first crossing never arrived — the desk holds 161 files and none is it.** Re-crossed as
`field-dispositions-recross-for-cowork-44dd210e1a213084.json`, file sha256
`44dd210e1a2130847190f034cf0005f83c413ef42b88b9b231dff9e5526db498`, 115 paths generated from the
live constants, eleven conformance cases, and the first artefact to carry the R726 mark.

**"Digest inline" resolved honestly**: a file cannot contain its own digest, so what is inline is
the digest of the MEMBERSHIP PAYLOAD — `membershipSha256` over a canonical serialisation of
`{theMembership, theRulesThatAreNotLists}`, recomputable on arrival over the same subtree, which
is the value an importer actually needs. The file digest travels where it must, in the staging
line and the sidecar.

**AND THE CONVENTION IS NAMED, because the default is wrong.** Checking that digest with Python's
default `json.dumps` FAILS: `ensure_ascii=True` escapes the em dashes and apostrophes in the rule
text and the digest moves. **I raised exactly that false alarm against my own artefact before
naming the spec** — the fault Cowork has already recorded once as *"six false alarms from my
instrument, about a file that was intact."* The artefact now states
`sort_keys=True, separators=(",",":"), ensure_ascii=False, UTF-8` — Cowork's own declared
digestSpec, restated so the default cannot bite — and records that it reproduces under that spec
and not under the other, *"a property of the convention rather than of the bytes."*

## R729 — A digest crosses with the serialisation that produces it

**Ruled (David, 2026-08-25), on the desk's confirmation that the membership recomputed and agrees
exactly at `2ae669ad510adb948b01db43bf95211b18ab3aa4fd909ed5aac8a047f59e33d0`: a digest crosses
with the serialisation that produces it, or the receiving party checks a different number.**

A hash is not a property of a value; it is a property of a value AND a spelling of that value.
`{a:1}` sorted or unsorted, spaced or not, with non-ASCII escaped or literal, are four different
byte strings and four different digests, all honestly computed over "the same data". **Naming the
convention is what made verification possible** — the desk agreed only because the artefact said
`sort_keys=True, separators=(",",":"), ensure_ascii=False, UTF-8`.

The evidence is on both sides of the same file: **it reproduces under that spec and NOT under
Python's default**, and I raised that false mismatch against my own artefact before naming it —
the fault Cowork had already recorded once as *"six false alarms from my instrument, about a file
that was intact."* Two stores have now hit it independently, which makes it a class rather than a
slip. **Every digest this store crosses names its serialisation from here.**

## R730 — The twenty-nine ruled; the notation thread closes

**Ruled: the twenty-nine are ANSWER SLOTS — notation, exempt, and nothing amends.** Cowork
answered from the carriers, **two mechanical facts per row, uniform**, which is the form this
question deserved: a claim about what a string IS, settled by what the row does with it, not by
reading the string and judging its tone.

**The notation thread closes** with its boundary intact across four rulings: orthography is not
emphasis (R716); the exemption needs a symbol-bearing path AND a symbol-shaped string (R719); gap
markers are exempt wherever they sit, because the sentence is where the gap must appear (R722);
and stimulus words are not, because they sit inside a sentence a child reads (R723). Answer slots
join the first class. **A bare shout in a stem can still claim none of it**, which is the probe
that keeps the whole thread honest.

## R731 — A name that claims a hash its bytes no longer have

**My own fault, found within one run of building the rule that caused it.** R726 marks every
emission at the door, injecting `instrumentProvenance` into the file. On its first run the mark
rewrote the file AFTER `stampedName` had hashed it, so **the artefact's name declared a content
hash the bytes no longer had** — and the name is how this store's superseding, retention and
family-matching all work (R602). **A mechanism built to honour one rule broke another on its
first execution**, which is the ordinary shape of a fix and the reason a fix is not finished when
it works.

Closed at the door rather than in the caller: `restampToContent` re-derives the stamp from the
ACTUAL bytes and renames the file, printing `restamped →` when it does, so the invariant holds
for every future emitter without anyone remembering it. **The general form: a derived name is a
CLAIM ABOUT CONTENT, so anything that may touch content must run before the name is fixed, or the
name must be re-derived after.** Ordering is not a detail where a name asserts a fact.

## R732 — Happened-to-be-safe is not provably-safe

**My own audit, against my own precedent, prompted by Cowork's migration order.** R717 deleted
`check:every-string-field`'s `DISPOSITIONS` map and its `isScreened` predicate **in the same edit
that added the import**, and verified afterwards. It worked. But the order Cowork proposed —
replacement lands, replacement is proven against its fixture, only then the predecessor leaves —
would have made it **provably** safe, and what I did was **happened-to-be** safe. The two are
indistinguishable from the outcome and distinguishable in the method, which is the whole
distinction this register exists to keep.

**Both of this turn's findings came from turning a new rule on old work** — the marking rule
exposed the stamp fault in the same run, and Cowork's migration order exposed my simultaneous
swap a week after it landed. That is the cheapest audit available here: **a new rule is a query
against everything already built**, and running it backwards costs one pass and finds faults
nobody was looking for. It found two today, and both were mine.

## R734 — A screen stricter than the gate finds the gate's exemptions and calls them faults

**Mine, in an instrument written the same turn as the rule it broke.** The walk-script screen's
first version called `checkChildFacingText` directly on the script instead of calling the item
gate. That omits every exemption the gate takes FROM THE ROW — the words the item tests, the
option words a script may legitimately name, the declared quotations, the passage's proper nouns.

**It reported three faults, TWO OF THEM ON LIVE ROWS, and all three are CLEAN at the gate**:
`ENG-003-A-SP-06` and `SP-09` name the misspelling they exist to test (*dictionery* / *Dictionary*),
and `ENG-019-BV-02`'s *quick* sits inside a declared quotation. Two LIVE items would have crossed
as carrying faults they do not have.

**And correcting it moved the answer in BOTH directions**: the 3 false faults went, and **8 real
ones appeared that the narrower call could not see at all**, because `internal-id-leak` comes from
the gate's own orphan-option check and never from `checkChildFacingText`. A narrower instrument is
not a stricter one — it is a DIFFERENT one, wrong in both directions at once. Caught by checking
the three against the gate before they crossed, which is the only reason this is a finding rather
than an incident. **Third instance of R717's class in four days, and all three were mine.**

## R735 — A zero from a narrow instrument is a fact about the instrument wearing a fact about the corpus

**Cowork's finding, registered in its words, and it belongs exactly where David placed it —
beside the 1,533 and the expiring fixture.** All three are the same shape: an instrument reports
about itself in language that reads as a report about the corpus.

- **The 1,533** (R714/R717): a re-derived predicate produced a figure that described the model,
  not the gate.
- **The expiring fixture** (R721): a self-test anchored to the standing corpus goes dark when the
  corpus is repaired — the instrument's silence reading as the corpus's cleanliness.
- **The zero from a narrow instrument** (this): a screen that never looked at a field reports no
  faults in it, and "no faults found" is indistinguishable from "nothing was looked at" unless
  the instrument states its own scope.

**The defence is the same in all three and this store already runs it: state the population, state
the method, state what the instrument cannot see — before the figure.** A number without its
denominator and its blind spots is a claim about a corpus made of evidence about a tool.

## R737 — A search that reads a serialisation reports a clean corpus and an empty one identically

**Register-grade and general (David, 2026-08-26), filed beside its narrow-instrument twin.**
Checking the joins-with prompts, a first pass tested `JSON.stringify(stem)` and reported **0
shouted AND 0 quoted** — the escaping had made `"tooth"` into `\\"tooth\\"` and the pattern matched
neither. The corpus was clean and the search said nothing was there; **a corpus with the fault and
a corpus with nothing in it produce the same output**, and only the second number's oddity —
zero of BOTH — exposed it.

**The rule: search the VALUE, never a rendering of it.** A serialisation adds escapes, reorders
keys, elides undefined and changes the bytes a pattern is matched against, so a regex over
`JSON.stringify` is a question asked of the encoder rather than of the data. The family it joins:
the re-derived predicate (R717), the expiring fixture (R721), the narrow call (R734) and the
narrow instrument (R735) — **five ways an instrument reports about itself in language that reads
as a report about the corpus**, and the same defence answers all five: state the population, the
method, and what the instrument cannot see, before the figure.

## R738 — A narrower instrument is not a stricter one: it is a different one, wrong both ways at once

**The canonical statement of the class, taken from its third instance (David, 2026-08-26).** The
formulation the register keeps:

> **A narrower instrument is not a stricter one — it is a DIFFERENT one, wrong both ways at
> once.**

**The proof is the correction itself: one change removed three false faults and revealed eight
real ones.** The walk-script screen called `checkChildFacingText` instead of the item gate, so it
lost every exemption the gate takes from the row — and reported `SP-06`, `SP-09` (both LIVE) and
`BV-02` as faulty when all three are clean, the first two naming the misspelling they exist to
test and the third quoting inside a declared quotation. The same narrowness could not see
`internal-id-leak` at all, because that verdict comes from the gate's orphan-option check, so
**eight genuinely stale scripts were invisible to it.**

Three instances in four days — R717's re-derived predicate, R734's narrow call, and this — **and
all three were mine**, which is the part worth keeping: the class is not a thing careless people
do, it is what building a second implementation always does, and the only reliable defence is to
call the family's own function rather than to write a careful copy of it.

## R739 — The frame is one token; key letters are mentions; and the split was a port wearing my name

**Her two rulings landed across the template** (`annie-161-landing-4ea1f1e72e5c3cbe.json`, file
sha256 `4ea1f1e72e5c3cbef6f52c11101832e4be33eb6bfcdb19f2749610344bb9c166`, findings digest inline
with its serialisation named): **40 of 40 vr-06 walk scripts amended**, both of her worked
examples reproducing byte-for-byte from the mechanical rule — *“out” makes “shout”*, *“pri” fills
it to make “deprive”*. **Per-row assertions as instructed**: every frame token present after the
edit and identical to before, and a mask-and-compare proving that NOTHING BUT the mention runs
moved. Units stated: **her ninety is the authoring source, this side holds 40 serving rows of the
template** (R690), and the ruling was applied to the whole template here rather than to the
twenty she read — her own *"a ruling that stays where it was made is a preference."*

**THE PREDICATE FINDING, and it is the sharpest form of R738 yet: `capitalRunIsExempt` DOES NOT
SPLIT.** Called directly on her three rows, the whole frame is exempt AND so is the leading letter
run — `SH___`, `DE___VE`, `COM___E`, `DEC___E`, every one a single span with the letters inside
it, because the pattern takes letters on both sides of the underscores. **The split came from
`build_ninety_screen.py over walkscript_screen.py` — Cowork's PYTHON PORT — and every split
verdict in that artefact carries `by: "capitalRunIsExempt(...) === false"`, attributing the
verdict to this function's NAME.** So a fault in a re-implementation reached the reviewer as
evidence about my code, and she ruled against my predicate for a behaviour it does not have.

**A second implementation wearing the original's name is the worst member of the class**, because
the misattribution is invisible to everyone downstream: the artefact is honest, the name is
accurate as a citation of intent, and the verdict is wrong. What I cannot settle from here —
whether the port predates R722 or mis-ports it — is NAMED rather than guessed; I hold no version
of that Python. **Her three rows are now regression tests**, so the split cannot be introduced
here later, and the predicate crosses with five conformance cases so neither store re-derives it.

**The option-value ruling needed no change and is recorded with its proof**: `options[].value`
already sits in `NOTATION_BEARING_PATHS` and `OUT` is symbol-shaped, so the 240 were exempt
before the ruling arrived — and the boundary still holds, because a sentence in that same field
cannot claim it (R719).

## R740 — A guard that compares totals refuses a pre-existing fault as if the edit caused it

**Mine, caught mid-run.** The substitution's safety guard gated the whole item after the edit and
threw on `bank-vr-06-missing-word-15` — whose *"poorly"* sits in the STEM and fails the ban list
**before anything is touched**. The edit was innocent; the guard blamed it.

**Refuse on the DIFF, never on the total** (R149, arriving in a new place): the guard now takes
the gate's verdict before and after and refuses only what the edit INTRODUCED. Pre-existing
faults are carried onto the row as `preExistingFaultsUntouchedByThisEdit` instead of stopping the
run — **three rows carry them** (`-15`, `-17`, `-40`), which is a finding the totals-guard would
have converted into a crash and lost. A guard that cannot tell what it caused from what it found
reports the corpus's history as its own damage.

## R741 — A verdict citing another party's function names the implementation that produced it

**The misattribution class, in my words, registered as the worst member of the second-implementation
family (R738):**

> **A verdict citing another party's function names THE IMPLEMENTATION THAT PRODUCED IT, never the
> function it ports. A port that cites the original is claiming an authority its own code has to
> earn — and the citation reads as accurate, which is precisely why it is the worst member.**

Every other member of the family announces itself eventually: a re-derived predicate disagrees
with the gate, an expiring fixture goes quiet, a narrow call misses a rule. **This one arrives
pre-endorsed.** The artefact was honest, the `by:` string was a truthful statement of intent, and
the verdict was wrong — so a fault in a Python port travelled to the reviewer as evidence about my
TypeScript, and she ruled against a behaviour my predicate does not have. **Nobody in the chain
could have caught it by reading carefully; only by running the cited function.**

**So the rule has a mechanical half**: a verdict that cites a function must be reproducible BY
THAT FUNCTION, and where two stores cannot see each other's code, the disagreement is settled by
**running both over shared inputs in a shared row shape** — not by comparing descriptions. That
artefact is `predicate-verdicts-side-by-side-17cb19fef347c6f3.json`, file sha256
`17cb19fef347c6f34c618d0b92502d697a57ff76d1ad509ae047c29a74a59d01`: this predicate's verdicts over
the exact twenty rows the port ran on, plus her four frames span by span. **80 runs compared, 60
agree, 20 disagree — and every disagreement is the same shape**, the port saying LOOSE where this
predicate says EXEMPT, every one a letter run sitting inside a frame token. The artefact asserts
nothing about the port's source, which this side does not hold.

## R745 — A conformance suite that avoids the boundary proves agreement about the interior only

**The finding that outlives the disagreement, and it indicts my own suite.** The eleven

## R746 — Retention lives inside the artefact being changed

**Ruled: a retention STORE is a convenience beside the thing; the before-image belongs ON THE
ROW**, where it travels with every copy, survives a directory clean, and cannot be separated from
the value it explains. `content/retention/` keeps its job for whole superseded FILES; **a changed
FIELD keeps its predecessor in the record that changed.**

**65 before-images backfilled** onto the walk scripts amended under R739/R742, each asserted
against its landing artefact's `after` before stamping — *a before-image written against a row
that has moved on is a false record, which is worse than none* — and against the artefact's own
declared digest for the `before`. They land as `_walkScriptBefore`, which **R715's underscore rule
classifies as retention automatically**: the gate skips them, no repairer touches them, and no
new disposition was needed. Verified after: 335 LIVE items still failing 0, dispositions still
UNDECLARED 0.

## R747 — A generated artefact declares its generator, and a check asserts they agree

**Her §4 ruled and wired.** Six rows drifted from their generator in the authoring store with no
record, and **nobody would know but for an unrelated search**. Her consequence is the operative
one: **a generated bank that no longer matches its generator has two sources of truth and no way
to say which is authoritative** — an amendment landed only in the bank is erased by the next
generation, and one landed only in the generator never reaches the rows that serve.

`pnpm check:generator-agreement`, wired into CI, asserts BOTH halves and calls `GENERATORS` — the
generator's own exported registry — rather than re-deriving what it would produce (R738):

- **DECLARATION**: it found **0 of 514 generated rows naming a generator.** They carried
  `authoredBy: ai-draft:claude-fable-5` — a MODEL, not a generator, and a model cannot be re-run
  to check a row. All 514 now declare
  `generator:packages/db/prisma/generate-content.ts#GENERATORS['<type>']`.
- **AGREEMENT**: **514 of 514 reproduce byte for byte**, including the R723 prompts, because that
  amendment landed in the generator AND the rows — which is exactly the discipline her ruling
  requires and the reason this side has no drift to report.

Drift is REPORTED, never repaired: which side is authoritative is a ruling, and an amendment may
legitimately live in the row.

## R748 — The ruling is on the SPEC: gapMarkerSpans returns the frame token

**Ruled on the definition rather than on either predicate (David, 2026-08-26), which is the only
place a ruling could settle this**: `gapMarkerSpans` **RETURNS THE FRAME TOKEN — LETTERS AND
UNDERSCORES TOGETHER**, and `frameTokenSpans` folds into it. **There is no second concept: a
`frameTokenSpans` sitting beside a narrower `gapMarkerSpans` is the divergence itself given two
names**, which is exactly what the port's own half printed — both spans, side by side, with the
predicate reading the narrower one.

**This side already returned the token; what changed is that the definition now SAYS so**, in the
place a future port reads. **The older meaning was portable precisely because nothing written
down contradicted it** — the spec was silent and both readings were defensible, so the port was
not wrong to read it that way, and no amount of care at the porting end could have settled it.
The definition now states the token's shape: any run of underscores together with the capital
letters immediately adjacent on either side, plus the optional `(n)` of a numbered cloze marker —
`SH___`, `___AN`, `DE___VE`, `___(2)___` each ONE span.

**Re-crossed with the corrected definition and its boundary cases**:
`field-dispositions-recross-for-cowork-62e62d3375276143.json`, file sha256
`62e62d33752761435346e7f4bbb21a3d770a4a3fbe0d9d78c6e7fe5224265457`, 115 paths, 19 conformance
cases. **The membership digest MOVED — `2ae669ad…` → `ed7813fc…` — and that is the digest working**:
the paths did not change, the RULES subtree did, and a digest over meaning must move when meaning
does. A crossing whose digest had stayed put would have been carrying a changed definition under
an unchanged name.

**One authority for who owns a type, while here**: `BANK_OWNED_TYPES` is now exported from the
generator and imported by `check:generator-agreement`, which previously would have inferred
ownership from an id prefix — a second definition of the same fact, in a check written to close
exactly that class. It now reports the skip explicitly: vr-02 and vr-06 are bank-owned.

## R749 — The rejected variant is not on this side, and cannot reappear here

**"The rest make real words with a poor meaning." appears NOWHERE in this repository** — not in
`generate-content.ts`, not in any bank this side holds, and on **no serving row** (checked across
every item's stem and explanation). **And it cannot reappear here on regeneration**: vr-06 sits in
`BANK_OWNED_TYPES`, so the generator skips it entirely and this side has **zero `gen-vr-06` rows**
— its vr-06 population is the bank's. The removal is the authoring store's to make in its own
generator; there is nothing here to remove, and this is stated rather than performed so that a
"done" does not travel for an act that never happened.

**Her cause is the finding worth keeping**: *"somebody refused one variant of ten and never
replaced it, and four rows filled the hole four different ways"* — four of six drifts, one cause.
**Her third clause on refusal-routing (R712): a refusal that removes something in use must name
its replacement or its owner. Silence after a rejection does not stop the work; it distributes
the authoring.**

## R750 — Provenance names what can be re-run

**Ruled general (David, 2026-08-26) from the model-versus-builder finding:**

> **Provenance names what can be RE-RUN. A model is not a generator; a name that cannot be
> executed against the row it explains is a label, not a provenance.**

All 514 generated rows carried `authoredBy: ai-draft:claude-fable-5` and every one of them read as
provenanced. But a model cannot be re-run to reproduce a row: the same prompt gives a different
answer, so the field asserted an origin nothing could check. **514 now name
`generator:packages/db/prisma/generate-content.ts#GENERATORS['<type>']`, and that is the form** —
a builder, addressable, executable, and asserted against the rows by `check:generator-agreement`
in CI, which reproduces all 514 byte for byte.

**The general test to apply to any provenance field: can the thing named be run against the row?**
If not, it records who to ask, which is worth having and is a different fact — and the two must
not share a column, because one of them supports a check and the other only a conversation.

**Her §4 confirmed and verified rather than assumed**: a reconstructed before-image may never
occupy a `replacedSha256` field, because that field asserts the row's actual prior bytes and a
round trip proves consistency, not identity. **Checked here**: the 65 before-images stamped under
R746 came from landing artefacts recording the ACTUAL prior strings, each hash verifying against
its own bytes, none reconstructed. This side is clean on the rule and the check is recorded rather
than the assumption.

## R751 — The forty hold: the frame has no accessible text, and that is the answer

Annie flagged that **the frame-versus-prose split may be an accessibility difference wearing a
quality one**, and that staging the forty without that fact risks her ruling the accessible form
out of the corpus. David held the forty until each row carries its frame's accessible text, or
states that none exists.

**None exists, on all forty.** Every `vr-06-missing-word` stem holds exactly two keys — `prompt`
and `sentence` — and no accessibility-shaped field exists anywhere on the type: no `accessibleText`,
no spoken form, no `ariaLabel`, no `alt`. The renderer adds none: `engines/stowaway.tsx` gives the
sentence a bare `<p>`. Its `Word` component *does* carry `role="img"` with an `aria-label`, and
that is the letter-tile path; the vr-06 sentence does not use it. So the one surface that could
speak the frame is not on this row's path.

**The consequence for her ruling, stated rather than assumed**: the frame/prose distinction both
stores have been ruling on is, today, VISUAL ONLY. A child using a screen reader receives the same
undifferentiated character stream for the frame as for the prose around it, so the exemption that
protects the diagram protects nothing they can hear — how `SH___` is voiced is the reader's
punctuation setting, which the product neither sets nor knows. **That does not make the ruling
wrong** — a diagram a sighted child reads is still a diagram — but the accessible form has never
existed rather than having been ruled against, and her flag is correct on the evidence. What would
change it is an authored spoken form per row saying what the frame IS. This store does not author
it. Crossed as `frame-accessible-text` (findings `90af1b57…`), one row per item.

## R752 — A digest names the keys as they appear in the file

`findingsSha256` crossed with `subtree: '{control, summary, divergence, strings}'` over a document
whose keys are `THE_CONTROL_ANSWERS_FIRST`, `theSummary`,
`THE_DIVERGENCE_IS_IN_gapMarkerSpans_NOT_IN_THE_PREDICATE`, `strings`. **Cowork verified it by
guessing among four candidate readings; one reproduced.** It got the right answer by luck, and the
next reader guesses wrong and refuses an honest artefact — the expensive direction, because a false
refusal costs a crossing and a crossing costs days here.

R729 named the SERIALISATION so the far side computes the same number over the same bytes. This is
the other half: **name the SELECTION.** A spec has both or it has neither, because a reader who
cannot assemble the subtree never reaches the question of how to serialise it.

The selection is no longer written by hand. `findingsDigest(payload, keys)` in
`scripts/lib/findings-digest.ts` takes the literal key names, **THROWS if any is not a top-level key
of the payload** — so an alias fails at the emitting door rather than at the receiving one — and
returns the `howToCheckThisOnArrival` block, so the names declared are necessarily the names hashed.
Three emitters carried aliases (`emit-port-crossing-half`, `land-annie-161`, `screen-walkscripts`);
`emit-predicate-verdicts` and the membership crossing were already correct. The port half re-crossed
as `d6899c72…` and its digest now reproduces mechanically from its own declaration.

## R753 — A case block riding inside a larger artefact shares that artefact's fate

The eight boundary cases were authored at R745 and put inside the membership crossing, where they
**twice failed to arrive**: Cowork reports the crossed membership still holds its original eleven,
and aliased `frameTokenSpans`/`isExemptByFrame` rather than deleting them because *a migration
proved against the wrong fixture is proved against nothing*. So they cross alone, small enough to be
run rather than read (`boundary-conformance-cases-for-cowork`, `164c68d1…`), with Cowork's own eight
run through this implementation in the same file — the thing that lets its alias names go, since it
cannot prove its port against cases it authored itself. **All eight of its expectations reproduce
here, span for span.**

**And its suite caught a class mine lacks.** *TWO marks in one string* — `"From SH___ to ___AN."` —
is a case **a single-match implementation passes every one of my eight and fails**. My four span
cases each carry exactly one mark. So the suite I authored to close a blind-agreement finding was
itself blind, one axis over: **a boundary suite is not finished when it reaches the boundary.** Mine
reached the seam between letters and underscores, which was the disagreement, and never asked
whether there could be TWO seams. **Coverage of a class is not coverage of its cardinality.** The
case is carried as the ninth, credited to Cowork.

## R754 — The name is not a verification surface; the sidecar is

`restampToContent` built its pattern out of the `family` label and **returned the path unchanged and
silent when the label and the filename disagreed**. So `deliver(…, 'boundary-conformance-cases')` on
`boundary-conformance-cases-for-cowork-<hash>.json` skipped the restamp, and the artefact staged
under a name claiming a hash its bytes did not have — the R731 fault re-entering through the
function built to prevent it, by the R87 route: an operation that is correct, a report that is true,
and neither saying that nothing happened. The prefix now comes from the FILENAME, and a label that
does not match its file is reported rather than obeyed.

**Then the sweep, and the number to distrust.** 117 of 168 stamped names at the door disagree with
their bytes. That reads as catastrophic and is not: **the 16 hex in a stamped name is not one
convention.** Some emitters stamp the file digest, others a payload digest or a batch id — one stamp
sits on TEN files, which no file digest could. My sweep had assumed uniformity and found a fault in
its own premise (R173, on my own instrument). **Every sidecar agrees with its bytes: 109 of 109,
zero disagreements.** So the sidecar is the only verification surface here and is the one with a
guard on it — `pnpm check:staged-digests`, which asserts the sidecar and explicitly does NOT check
the name, saying so on every run. 126 older artefacts carry no sidecar: unverifiable, which is a
different thing from corrupted, and reported as its own line.

## R755 — The exempted population, walked: the split is by renderer, not by quality

Annie's accessibility flag ruled open on channel. **Nobody rules a remedy until the population is
known**, so every string in the corpus claiming a notation exemption was walked and reported per
row. It calls the gate's own walker (`textsFrom`), the disposition membership and the two exemption
predicates themselves; the one thing it cannot get from a function is which RENDERER a path
reaches, so the render map is declared with the file and line each entry was read from, and any
`(engine, path)` not in it reports **UNKNOWN, never "none"** (R98). The family→engine map is read
out of `play-runner.tsx` rather than hand-kept (R57) — `cloze` reuses the word-web component, and a
hand-written map would have put cloze gaps on an unread renderer and reported UNKNOWN for **the one
class that does name its gaps**.

**289 exempt strings across 1,037 items, 187 LIVE.** Not 349, and the instrument was not tuned
until it agreed. The predicate is stated instead: a string where the exemption is LOAD-BEARING —
it carries a run the shouted-capitals rule would otherwise fail, or an underscore marker that would
otherwise be screened. The first run returned **3,470**, of which 3,376 were option values, because
`notationExempt` is true of any single-token value including `cat`: **exempt in the sense that a
locked door is keeping out somebody who was not coming.** Counts under four readings are crossed so
the 349 can be located by its predicate rather than by its size (R591).

**And the answer is not uniform, which is why walking it mattered.** Reporting "none exists"
corpus-wide from the forty would have been false:

| class | rendered to a child | substitute accessible text |
|---|---|---|
| GAP_MARKER, cloze carrier | 16 | **16 name themselves** — `splitCarrierAtGaps` hides the marker and adds "gap N" (R668) |
| GAP_MARKER, `quotes[].text` | 0 — no child surface renders it | n/a |
| FRAME | 60 | **0** |
| OPTION_VALUE | 195 | 0, and **not one carries an underscore** — every one is ordinary letters |

**The class her flag is about is 60 rows, 51 LIVE, and it is one question type.** Every rendered
string whose exempt token contains characters that do not speak is `vr-06-missing-word`: the forty
`stem.sentence` frames already held, and twenty `explanation.walkScript` frames on the same rows.
Nothing in maths, NVR, comprehension or SpaG is in it. **The split is not by quality and not by
district — it is by which renderer the path reaches, and exactly one renderer in the corpus was
ever built to name a marker.** Membership only; no remedy is proposed and none is implied.

## R756 — A command that cannot fail has not run

`npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json | grep …; echo "typecheck ok"` — there is no root
`tsconfig.json`. tsc emitted TS5058 and exited non-zero; the grep filtered it out, the pipeline's
status was the grep's, and the unconditional `echo` supplied a verdict **derived from nothing**.
Two real errors sat behind it, both introduced by the edit that turn, and both found only when the
repo's own `pnpm typecheck:scripts` was run instead.

**The fault is not the missing file — it is that the sentence "typecheck ok" was written by me
rather than by the command.** A verdict must be the exit status of the thing it describes. So:
invoke the repo's NAMED script, never an ad-hoc reconstruction of it (the named one is where the
config is wired, which is R57's lesson in shell form); never `echo` a verdict after a pipeline, as
`|` discards the status of everything but the last stage; and when a command is expected to print
nothing on success, that silence is only evidence if the command could have spoken.

**The family, now four deep.** R60's zero, R61's absent population, R87's silent no-op and R80's
wrong clock are all instruments that say nothing while appearing to say something. This one is
worse in one specific way and better in another: the verdict was not the instrument's at all, so no
discipline aimed at the instrument could have caught it — and it is the cheapest to prevent, since
the guard is to stop writing the answer down yourself.

**IT GENERALISES PAST THE BUILD TOOL, AND IT BELONGS BESIDE THE EMPTY-JOIN FAMILY.** The shape is
not "tsc" and not "a missing config" — it is **an operation whose failure mode is silence, wearing a
verdict its operator wrote.** A join on a key that matches nothing returns no rows and raises
nothing; a filter on a renamed field selects nothing and raises nothing (R568); `str.replace` on a
mismatched anchor changes nothing and raises nothing (R87); a gate over a population no path
produces screens nothing and exits 0 (R60, R61). Every one is an operation that CANNOT FAIL,
because failing is not among the things it does. **The pipeline case adds the last step: `|`
discards the status of every stage but the last, so even an operation that CAN fail stops being
able to once it is piped.** Hence the general form, which is testable before running anything:
*name the specific observation that would make this command report failure.* If there is none, the
command is not evidence and its silence is not a pass.

Two mechanical consequences: invoke the repo's NAMED script rather than an ad-hoc reconstruction of
it (the named one is where the config is wired — R57 in shell form), and never write a verdict
sentence after a pipeline, because the sentence is then yours and not the command's.

**And R757 carries the other self-finding**, which was folded into R754's second half and is large
enough to stand alone.

## R757 — R731 re-entering through the function built to prevent it

`restampToContent` exists for exactly one purpose: to stop an artefact staging under a name that
claims a hash its bytes no longer have (R731, the stamp-after-mark fault). **It reintroduced that
fault itself.** It built its match pattern out of the `family` label passed to `deliver()`, so when
the label and the filename prefix disagreed — `deliver(…, 'boundary-conformance-cases')` on a file
named `boundary-conformance-cases-for-cowork-<hash>.json` — the pattern missed, the function
**returned the path unchanged and printed nothing**, and the artefact crossed under a false stamp.

**Three properties made it invisible.** The function was correct on every file whose label matched.
It printed nothing on the ones it skipped, so the log of a bad run and a good run were identical.
And the failure was in the guard rather than in the thing guarded, so every downstream check stayed
green — a guard reports on its subject, never on itself.

**The fix is a rule about where a fact comes from, not a patched regex**: the prefix is read from
the FILENAME, which is the artefact, and never from the label, which is a caller's description of
it. A mismatch between the two is now reported rather than obeyed. Same shape as R57 (a door that
enumerates what it expects will drift from the thing it is describing) and R60's third question
(is it reading the artefact, or a copy of it?) — **the label was the copy.**

## R758 — R57 reached stems and never reached options

**Cowork named the risk in the abstract and it was concrete here.** Its ruling on what the 349 walk
must carry ended with: *a field authored there and dropped at your door is invisible to a walk of
serving rows, because the walk can only see what arrived.* That is exactly right, it is not
hypothetical, and it was true of this corpus until this turn.

`scripts/import-english-items.ts` rebuilt every option as
`{ value: option.content, ...(label) }` from an interface declaring four keys **with no index
signature**, so anything else authored on an option was dropped in silence — no warning, no count,
no trace on the row afterwards. Meanwhile `apps/web/lib/actions/admin-items.ts` takes
`content: z.record(z.unknown())` and passes everything through. **Two doors enumerating separately,
drifted.** R57 predicted this in the sentence that names it, R42 and R55 already recorded it once
each — and R57 was written about STEMS, so the option path was never brought under it.

**Measured, over the 19 files in that door's own input shape: 553 authored values on four keys.**
`misconceptionExecution` is 499 of them, and it is **a real column** the schema describes as *"the
first thing a reviewer asks to see"*. The comment beside `drafterDeclaredPull` in that same model
records this identical fault happening before — a door carried the tag, dropped the sentence, no
column held it, nothing said so at the crossing, and a reviewer spent three returns reconstructing
pulls by archaeology (R707). **The same fault, on a field that DID have a column to land in.**

**Fixed by adding the index signature, which is the mechanism rather than the symptom.** An unknown
key now reaches the row builder, where it is carried to its column if one exists (12 columns, read
from Prisma's own datamodel, never hand-listed — a list here would drift from the schema one level
above the fault being closed), carried into `content` if it is retention (`_`-prefixed), and
otherwise **REFUSES THE IMPORT BY NAME**. Nothing is dropped. Refusing rather than guessing a home
is deliberate: inventing a placement convention is how a second wrong convention starts (R173).
Of the 553, 531 now land in columns, 22 carry as retention, and 24 `secondaryMisconceptionId` stop
the import instead of vanishing.

**And the honest status of the walk, which this bounds.** The exempted-population walk is a true and
complete account of what is ON the serving rows. **It is not evidence about what was authored**, and
for options it could not have been. Anything dropped before now left nothing here to find. That
limit is carried in the artefact itself rather than in a covering note.

## R759 — Every digest names its own spec, not its neighbour's

`manifestSha256` sat one line below a `howToCheckThisOnArrival` block naming the R729 canonical-JSON
spec, and was computed over newline-joined TEXT. Annie recovered it by guessing among three
readings — **the second time in three turns a digest was verified by guesswork**, and R752 had
already closed exactly this for the subtree keys.

**The generalisation R752 missed: a spec block is not a property of the DOCUMENT, it is a property
of ONE DIGEST.** One block plus a second digest reads as a spec covering both, and PROXIMITY DOES
THE ASSERTING — which is the same shape as R204 (a qualifier one field over is not a qualifier) and
R608 (one decision split across two fields sorts as neither).

Wired at the emitter, as R752 was. `digestOverText` produces the value and its spec together, so
they cannot drift; `assertDigestsNameTheirSpec` refuses to stage any artefact whose top-level
`*Sha256` names no spec, and it is called from `deliver()` — the one door every artefact passes —
because the fault being closed was a spec that had to be remembered. **The guard was canaried
before being trusted (R756):** it refuses a synthetic specless digest and passes the real artefact.

## R760 — A crossing reported absent and later arriving in a batch is a latency fact, not a loss

Three artefacts were reported absent over three turns and then arrived together, three or four
copies of each, findings payloads byte-identical. **Nothing was lost and nothing was mis-sent; the
channel batches.** Registered so the next absence is read correctly: an artefact not at the door is
LATE until proven otherwise, and re-crossing it costs a filename, which is the right price to pay
for the ambiguity.

**And only the findings digests made it legible.** Four copies of one artefact under four names is
an unreadable pile without something that says *these are the same document*; the file digest
cannot do it, because renaming and re-marking change the bytes. **The findings digest, computed
over the payload and not the packaging, was stable across every re-crossing** — and that stability
is what turned four copies into one artefact seen four times. R752's key-naming is what made those
digests checkable at all, so the two rules are one mechanism: the digest identifies the content,
and naming its spec is what lets the far side confirm the identity rather than assume it.

## R761 — A repair that reaches one renderer has not reached the class

**Sixty rendered frames carry no accessible substitute; the sixteen that do are all on the one
renderer built under R668.** That is the finding, and it is not a remedy: no repair is proposed and
none is ordered — the reading belongs to a seat nobody has filled.

The shape is what generalises. R668 was a correct, complete, well-executed accessibility repair; it
named every gap in the cloze carrier and it is why 16 of 16 rendered gap markers speak. **It was
scoped to a renderer, and the property it established is a property of a CLASS** — a marker whose
visible form does not speak needs something that says what it is, wherever that marker renders.
Every other renderer carrying such a marker was outside the repair and stayed outside it, silently,
because nothing measures a class from inside a component.

**The tell is that the split runs along renderer boundaries and along nothing else** — not district,
not question type, not authoring vintage, not quality. When a property divides that way, the repair
was scoped to the mechanism instead of to the property, and the unrepaired remainder is invisible
until somebody walks the class. Sibling to R565, where a ruling applied to the field it was observed
on left the same ruling standing wrong in an unreviewed channel.

## R762 — Matching by label across copies that disagree wrote a distractor's rationale onto a key

**Mine, applied and reversed within the same run.** Landing R758's dropped option fields, I matched
authored options to rows by label, took whichever copy the walk reached first, and wrote 19
`misconceptionExecution` values onto options marked CORRECT. The column means *why THIS distractor
executes THIS misconception*; a key cannot have one, which is what made it visible. **Reversed to
NULL, restoring the prior state exactly** — the writes had only ever touched fields that were null,
so the reversal is identity and not a second guess.

**The cause was not the matcher, it was that no source was authoritative.** Two files named
`eng006-draft.json` sit in different directories and disagree about what option B of ENG-006-TM-02
IS and about which option is CORRECT. Measured across the authored files: **135 (item, label) pairs
disagree between copies, 48 of them about which option is the key, over 36 items.** CLAUDE.md's own
rule says to diff a batch against the DB before importing; I swept a directory tree instead, and a
sweep has no notion of authority.

**The script now refuses rather than choosing.** It records the shape of each `(itemId, label)`
identity as it collects, and exits naming the conflicting identities instead of landing anything —
because picking between disagreeing copies is a ruling, and a ruling is not a script's to make
(R173). **The re-import is BLOCKED, not failed**: it completes the moment an authoritative source
directory is named, and not before.

**And R758's figure is corrected.** I reported 553 authored values in the door's path. Deduplicated
by (item, option, key, value) it is **419**, and of those **288 were already present on the rows and
equal** — they had reached the database by another path. Only 21 were absent and landable, 2 of
which (`tagStatus` on ENG-004-AGG-07/08 distractors) are correct and stand. 76 more are present and
DIVERGED from the authored source, which is a two-store question and is reported, never overwritten.
**The door's fault was real; its exposure was a quarter of what I first said.** I published an
alarming number without checking whether the values were actually missing from the rows — the exact
inversion of R173, which warns that a confirming number needs investigating on purpose. An alarming
one does too.

## R763 — A two-bucket coverage report lies about the size of the uncovered set

Cowork found a class this store had no way to see: **224 authored child-facing strings on
`options[].value[]`, list-shaped option values on the vr-02 odd-pair template**, against a crossed
membership carrying `options[].content.value` and nothing of any name for a list.

**Its premise needs one correction and the correction is the finding.** The message reads *a value
with no shape to arrive in is an unbuilt path, not a dropped one, and it leaves no record at any
door.* At the STORAGE layer that is not what happened: `ItemOption.content` is a `Json` column, so
`{"value": ["van","bus"]}` lands without difficulty, and **100 vr-02 options hold exactly that
shape today — 200 strings, on rows, right now.** What is unbuilt is one layer up. `options[].content.value`
is declared child-facing and screened; `options[].content.value[]` **is declared nowhere**, so the
gate walks those 200 strings and screens **0**. The path arrived; the membership never did.

**And nothing reported it.** `check:every-string-field` prints `UNDECLARED 0` on every run and is
correct — it screens the 326 LIVE items behind a door, and all 25 vr-02 items are DRAFT. R61's
shape: a gate whose scope legitimately excludes the thing being asked about, printing a true zero.

**My own coverage report was the same fault one level down.** It split field paths into
yielded-rows and examined-and-clean, which reads as a complete account and is not — a path can be
present in the corpus and screened by NOTHING, and mine named the scalar option path as examined
while the list shape under it was invisible. **An unscreened path reported inside "examined" is the
uncovered set understating its own size.** A third bucket now carries them, and it is not one path:
**13 undeclared paths, 441 strings**, `options[].content.value[]` (200) the largest, `stem.wordWithGap`
(25) notable because it renders to a child in a bare `<p>`.

**The joinable key, since that was the operative question:** `itemId` (authored, stable, identical
on both sides) plus the ordered value tuple. **Not the option id** — all 100 are auto-minted cuids
that nothing on the authoring side could have produced — and not the label, because 0 of the 100
carry one. The count gap is reported and not reconciled: Cowork says 224, the rows hold 200, and the
join above is what settles the 24 rather than any argument from totals.

No column was built, no disposition declared, no gate widened. As instructed.

## R764 — A reply is not an artefact

The 553 re-import and the execution population were answered in a reply two turns running and
reported unanswered both times. **They were answered where answers do not cross.** This store
already holds the rule — R25: when a value carries a signature, send the value, not an account of
it; prose may accompany a value and may never stand in for one — and I broke it on the two figures
most likely to be quoted back.

**The tell was available and I did not read it.** Every artefact this store emits gets a digest, a
sidecar and a staging line precisely so its arrival can be confirmed; a figure in a chat reply has
none of those, so there is nothing for the far side to name and nothing for this side to check. The
same turn in which I registered R760 — that a crossing reported absent is a latency fact — I was
treating prose as a crossing that had no channel at all.

Both figures now cross as `three-open-answers`, with the vr-02 rows carried as data beside them.
**The general form: if an answer matters enough to be asked for twice, it is an artefact.**

## R765 — Which file wins is not which answer is right

I proposed naming an authoritative directory to unblock the re-import. **That is the wrong
instrument.** Naming a directory decides which FILE wins; it does not decide which ANSWER is right,
and on 24 items the two readings disagree about exactly that. A directory ruling would have settled
**48 content questions by provenance** — adopting whichever answer happened to sit in the folder
somebody named — and no amount of correct filing makes that a content decision. **The reviewer is
the only party who can settle which answer is right**, so the readings cross to her side by side
and nothing lands until she rules. The 19 reversed executions stay reversed and re-land only under
whichever reading she confirms.

**And my framing was wrong in a way that made the directory ruling look adequate.** I said *two
files named `eng006-draft.json` sit in different directories and disagree*, which sounds like a
filing problem between two drafts. **One of those directories is `~/Downloads/11+/from-cluecrew` —
THIS STORE'S OWN OUTBOUND.** All 24 key disagreements are the same single pairing: a copy this
store exported against a file this store did not produce. There are not two authoring copies in
play. And on **24 of 24, the serving row agrees with this store's export** — the export mirrors the
database, so it is one party with two faces, not two witnesses.

**The real statement is therefore much sharper: the database, and so what a child would meet,
disagrees with an authored source about which answer is right, on 24 items.** A two-party content
disagreement between the stores — not a drafting muddle, and not something a folder can decide.

**Two figures corrected in the same pass, both the same shape.** I reported *48 disagreements over
36 items*; it is 48 over **24** items. The 36 is items disagreeing about ANYTHING — 24 about the
answer, 12 about wording only. I attached the wider item count to the narrower pair count, which is
the 553's shape exactly: a true number under a label that widened it. Both classes cross, separated,
because a wording disagreement is also hers and is a different question.

## R766 — The rule caught me inside the artefact that carries it

The per-row digests on the disagreement rows declared the canonical-JSON spec and were computed
with `JSON.stringify(row, Object.keys(row).sort())`. **A replacer ARRAY is not a sort**: it filters
every nested object to the top-level key names and preserves insertion order. The declared spec did
not reproduce the digest, on any of the 36 rows.

**R759 was registered one turn earlier and its guard passed this artefact**, because
`assertDigestsNameTheirSpec` asks whether a spec is NAMED and cannot ask whether it is TRUE. That
is the correct limit for a cheap structural guard and it is worth stating rather than patching over:
naming a spec is checkable at the door; honouring it is only checkable by recomputing, which the
emitting side can do and the receiving side must do anyway.

**The repair is the same one R752 made for the subtree and R759 for the manifest — call the
function the spec names.** `canonicalJson` is now used directly, so the description and the
computation are the same object rather than two things kept in agreement by attention. All 36 rows
reproduce. **Third time in three turns that a digest and its stated spec drifted apart, and the
first time the drift was inside the artefact registering the rule against it.**

## R767 — An emitter recomputes its declared digests before crossing

Ruled from R766. **Naming a spec is checkable at the door; honouring it is only checkable by
recomputing** — and the emitting side is the only party that can recompute BEFORE the artefact
leaves. `assertDigestsNameTheirSpec` asked whether a spec was named and passed an artefact whose
36 row digests reproduced under none of them; that is the correct limit for a cheap structural
guard and the wrong place to stop.

`assertDeclaredDigestsRecompute` now runs inside `deliver()` — the one door every artefact passes —
and recomputes `findingsSha256` from its declared `subtreeKeys` and every `rowSha256` on every row,
throwing on any that does not reproduce. It prints what it checked (`recomputed: findingsSha256 +
38 row digest(s)`), because a guard that says nothing is indistinguishable from one that did not
run (R756). **A digest whose spec it cannot interpret is reported UNCHECKABLE rather than passed** —
an unverifiable digest is not a failure, but it must not read as a success.

## R768 — The key-dispute class is empty, and every one of them resolves without a judgement

Her method was ruled: per item, from stem and options alone, three outcomes with REFUSE where the
stem determines neither or both. **Classifying the population mechanically first, from the same two
inputs her method uses, the batch that method is for turns out to be EMPTY.** Of 38 items whose
readings differ:

| | |
|---|---|
| **DIFFERENT QUESTION** — the stems differ | **19** |
| **RELABELLING ONLY** — same keyed TEXT, different letter | **10** |
| **OPTION-SET DIVERGENCE** — one stem, different options | **7** |
| more than two readings | 2 |
| **KEY DISPUTE** — same stem, same options, different answer | **0** |

**Not one item is a case where the same question, offering the same choices, is given a different
answer.** The largest class is two different questions sharing an id — `ENG-006-TM-02` asks *what
does Uncle Podger DO straight after taking off his coat (lines 8 and 9)* in one reading and *what
does he SAY when the picture needs putting up (lines 6 and 7)* in the other. Each key is correct for
its own stem. **Her method cannot be applied there at all: it reads one stem, and there are two.**
And on 10 more, both readings key the SAME TEXT and differ only in the letter above it.

So *"24 items where the database disagrees with an authored source about which answer is right"* was
my third wrong framing of this population in as many turns — first a filing muddle, then a two-party
content disagreement, and now: **an id collision, a relabelling, and a genuinely separate class,
with no answer dispute anywhere in it.** Each reframing came from looking at one layer further in,
and the pattern is that I characterised the population before reading its members (R595).

**The rows all cross regardless, with the classification exposed so she can overrule any of it** —
a mechanical class is a reading of the data, not a ruling, and the seat that rules is hers.

**The blinding, and why the previous artefact would have leaked.** She asked not to know which
reading is which, because a label that leaks is a shortcut she cannot unsee. Removed: file paths,
directory names, store names, and **the serving row** — which the previous artefact carried marked
`NOT_A_VOTE`. That label is honest and *does not make it unreadable*: it identifies the database's
reading exactly. **An honesty label is not a blind.** Reading order is fixed by the sha256 of each
reading's own canonical JSON, so it is deterministic and uncorrelated with provenance — measured,
reading 1 is this store's copy on 15 of 38 rows (39%), where a systematic 0% or 100% would be
readable off the position alone. Nothing else was stripped: both stems and every option cross in
full. The unblinding map is held at `content/blinded-readings-unblinding.json` and is not staged.

**The nineteen executions stay reversed and RE-DERIVE from whichever key she settles**, rather than
being un-reversed — un-reversing would restore values computed against a key that has not been
ruled, which is the same fault that produced them.

Her finding, ruled. **Seventeen of twenty-four were label permutations with both sides agreeing on

| | |
|---|---|
| byte-identical | 61 |
| **label permutation only — identical under the text predicate** | **16** |
| numbering drift — the same stem wears a different id | 9 |
| stem unmatched | 10 |
| **option-set divergence — one stem, different options** | **8** |
| **key text differs — a real answer dispute** | **0** |

**The desk named six option-set divergences; this run finds eight** — estate-wide rather than

## R770 — An attempt stores neither a letter nor the text, and nothing holds the id it does store

`Attempt.chosenOptionId` holds the **ItemOption ROW ID** — a cuid. So a permutation that reassigns
LETTERS across the same rows leaves every recorded attempt meaning exactly what it meant, and the
question as posed is moot in that direction.

**It is not moot in the other.** `chosenOptionId` is a bare `String?` with **no foreign key, no
relation and no cascade** — and **six writers delete and recreate an item's options rather than
updating them**, including the CMS edit path (`admin-items.ts:126`), `generate-content.ts`,
`import-vr-banks.ts` and three vr deploy scripts. Any of those re-mints the ids, and every attempt
on that item is left pointing at a row that no longer exists. **Nothing reports it because nothing
can: there is no constraint to violate.**

**Membership today: 5 attempts recorded, 5 carrying a chosen option, 0 that fail to resolve, 0 items
affected.** And that zero is a measurement of how little has happened yet, not evidence the design
holds — R62's lesson exactly. Five attempts is a pre-production table, which makes now the cheap
moment to put a key on the column or an update-in-place path on the options. Not built; reported.

## R771 — The numbering drift is its own class, and it is not a content fault

Reported ahead of any content reading, because reading it as content is the error it invites.
**Nine items are the same question wearing a different id.** `ENG-005-BB-02` through `BB-08` are an
**off-by-one chain** — each stem appears one position over in the other file, seven consecutive
items shifted as a run. `ENG-007-LP-07` and `LP-09` are a straight swap: *"What did Reuben do with
the folded paper from his pocket? (lines 34 to 36)"* is LP-07 in one file and LP-09 in the other.

**The ten "unmatched" stems are reported UNKNOWN, not as differences.** A stem that differs and
appears under no other id in the compared file is consistent with a genuinely different question OR
with the tail of a shift whose counterpart is absent — and **the BB run ends exactly where these
begin**, which is what makes assigning them a guess (R98).

**And the blinding gained a salt.** Ordering readings by their own content hash is uncorrelated with
provenance per row but not across rows: measured, reading 1 was the same store on 7 of 8 rows. On
eight rows that is chance and it is still a thread — deduce one row and the rest lean the same way.
Salting the sort with the item id makes each row's order independent of every other's; measured
after, 4 of 8. **A blind that holds per row and leaks in aggregate is not a blind**, and the only
reason I saw it was checking the distribution rather than the mechanism.

## R772 — The constraint goes on now, because five attempts is the cheapest this will ever be

`Attempt.chosenOptionId` was a bare `String?` — no relation, no cascade, **nothing to violate** —
while six writers delete and recreate an item's options rather than updating them. A foreign key is
now on it with **`ON DELETE RESTRICT`**, chosen over the alternatives for a specific reason:
`Cascade` would delete the history the column exists to hold, and `SetNull` would keep the row and
lose the answer, **which is the same silent loss one field over.** Restrict makes a delete that
would strand an attempt fail AT THE DELETE SITE. That is the whole property being bought.

**Canaried both ways before being trusted** (R756): deleting an option that carries an attempt is
refused with `Attempt_chosenOptionId_fkey`, and an option with no attempt still deletes. Migration
replay is clean and all 13 hand-written invariants still hold.

**What it costs, stated rather than discovered later.** 5 items now refuse an option delete, 1,032
do not. `content:generate` never reaches its delete on them — `writable` excludes reviewed rows —
and it mints deterministic option ids (`${id}-opt${n}`) anyway, so its recreate preserves referents.
**The path that will feel this is the CMS edit** (`admin-items.ts:126`), which deletes an item's
options and recreates them with fresh cuids: editing an item a child has attempted will now error.
Near-zero today; at volume it needs the update-in-place path, and that is the follow-on this buys
time for rather than replaces.

## R773 — Zero of 104, and the cause in Cowork's words

**The answer-dispute class is empty estate-wide: 0 of 104 items carried by two or more files.** Not
one has two readings offering the same options under the same stem and keying different TEXT. Every
apparent answer dispute in this thread was a label permutation, a numbering drift, or an option-set
divergence.

**The cause, in Cowork's words: four counts moved because the predicate got stated and applied
rather than inherited from the sentence carrying the number.** 553 → 419 distinct. 36 items → 24.
24 disputes → 0. 6 divergences → 8. Every one of those numbers was true when first written and
false by the time I repeated it, because what travelled between turns was the FIGURE and not the
PREDICATE THAT PRODUCED IT — and a figure with its predicate left behind will be applied to
whatever population the next sentence happens to be about.

**This is R591 and R25 meeting.** R591: a count needs its unit and its predicate, and a label
supplies neither. R25: send the value, not an account of it. **A count IS an account** — it is the
most compressed account there is, and compressing it is exactly what strips the predicate off.
The rule that follows: **a count crosses with the predicate that selected it, or it does not
cross.** Not the label, not the class name — the predicate, in terms someone could re-run.
