| `proportion` | 10 | **3** | no |
| `percentage` | 10 | 3 | no |

So the desk's *three words of ten or more letters* and the gate's *two* were both right about
different rules. **`proportion` is ten letters and three syllables**, and the gate was correct to
pass it. Then R338's dedup runs on top: distinct headwords, not tokens, with a word containing
another counted once.

**The name is the fault, not the rule.** *"2 distinct long word(s)"* invites a reader to check
lengths, and a reader who does will disagree with the gate every time a long word is short of
syllables. A rule whose name states a different predicate from its test will be re-litigated
forever by anyone who reads only its output.

**And the ruling: the cap binds the HINT role and not the notice class.** Same ground as the
sixteen-word cap — a child mid-item after a miss, reading under pressure. **A notice is not read
under pressure**: it is read once, at a door, with nothing riding on it. `notice` and `doorplate`
now carry `maxLongWords: null` — **null, not zero**, because zero would forbid every long word
rather than lift the cap.

**This is R689's second half.** That ruling gave the doorplate role no word cap and stance gates
only — and left `maxLongWords: 1` in place, because the role was minted by copying a row and its
caps came with it unexamined. **A role minted by copying inherits every cap nobody re-read**, and
the inheritance is invisible precisely because it was never decided.

## R869 — The face landed on her bytes, and the window is open by instruction

`The Ashline Working Register` and its description are on the case, **byte-identical as stored** —
title `88f99fae8ce3…`, description `e5235dc9585b…`, hashed after the write, not before. **She
approved a string and the string is what landed**: no normalised space, no stripped newline, no
"same wording".

**`caseFaceServes` is now TRUE, and the visible-but-empty window is OPEN.** 173 of 187 signed, **0
LIVE**, so the case is visible with nothing behind it. That is exactly the sequence R857 named as
the only one that opens the window — **and it is open by instruction, measured here rather than
discovered later.** It closes when the first item goes LIVE.

**Two notes on the prior.** The record at `content/case-faces/case-maths-01.json` correctly carries
no `_previous`: this is the first face ever landed on this case, so there was no prior face to stamp.
**But the DB's pre-face state — `narrativeIntro` holding the EMPTY-slot marker — was replaced
without retention.** The standing path retains prior FACES; it does not retain the state a case was
in before it had one. That is a small gap and it is named rather than repaired: the marker's content
is recorded verbatim at R861 and in the crossed artefact `b3918841…`, so nothing is lost this time.

## R870 — CORRECTION: the window is closed, and a face does not make a case visible

**My prose said the visible-but-empty window was OPEN. It is CLOSED, figure 0, and my own artefact's
blast radius said so.**

**A landed face makes a case RENDERABLE; a non-empty LIVE pool makes it VISIBLE.** `servableCaseIds`
derives visibility from the pool AT REQUEST TIME: `case-maths-01` has 0 LIVE+PRACTICE items, so it
does not render in the district map, is not selectable as a focus case, and cannot consume a
session. Measured: **16 of 28 cases servable; this one is not.**

**I conflated `caseFaceServes` with visibility**, and they are two different gates in series. The
face was the one I had just landed, so it was the one I reasoned from.

**And the fault I nearly reported as fine is the exact fault eleven PAID VR doors were hidden for**
(R695): a door that opens onto an ending, sitting in the default path. That rule is why the window
**cannot** open by landing a face — visibility is derived from the pool itself, so the combination
*visible AND empty* is unreachable rather than merely avoided. **A correct claim of OPEN would have
described a regression that R695 makes impossible.**

The artefact is corrected at `8140844360811c5e…`, and the correction runs the right way round: **the
artefact was right and the prose was wrong**, which is the opposite of the usual direction here and
worth recording for that reason alone.

## R871 — The rule is renamed to what it tests

`long-words` → **`four-syllable-words`**. The test is `syllables(word) >= 4` and has never counted
letters: `operations` and `percentages` count; `proportion` does not, and it is ten letters.

**The name was the fault.** *"2 distinct long word(s)"* sends every reader to count lengths, and a
reader who counts lengths disagrees with the gate whenever a long word is short of syllables — which
is precisely the disagreement the desk and this store just had. The message now reads *"distinct
word(s) of FOUR OR MORE SYLLABLES"*, and the reported words are stripped of trailing punctuation:
printing `operations,` made the gate look as though it matched punctuation and sent readers to count
the wrong string.

**A rule whose name states a different predicate from its test will be re-litigated by everyone who
reads only its output**, and the output is what most readers ever see.

## R872 — The state before there was a face is also a prior

`landCaseFace` retained prior FACES and nothing else, so the **first** landing on any case overwrote
whatever the slot held with no record of it. For `case-maths-01` that was a `narrativeIntro` carrying
the EMPTY-slot marker.

**Nothing was lost, and that was luck**: the marker's bytes had already crossed in another artefact
(R861), so the record existed somewhere else by coincidence of a different instruction. **A
retention that depends on the state having been copied elsewhere is not a retention.**

Wired: `_preFaceState` captures the ROW as it stood before the write, on **every** landing, whether
or not a prior face existed. On a first landing it is the only record that the slot was empty and
what it held instead.

**The distinction the old code missed is the one R842 already drew**: an empty prior is a STATE, not
an absence. `prior && prior.title` treated the empty string as "nothing to retain", and the one case
where retention matters most — the first landing, the only moment the pre-face state exists — was
the exact case it skipped.

## R873 — Two gates in series: a face makes a case RENDERABLE, a pool makes it VISIBLE

Registered as the distinction rather than the incident.

**`caseFaceServes` and `servableCaseIds` are two gates in series and neither implies the other.** A
landed face gives a case something to render; a non-empty LIVE+PRACTICE pool gives it a reason to
appear at all. A case with a face and no pool is absent from the district map. A case with a pool and
no face renders nothing. **Both must hold, and each is derived independently at request time.**

**The general fault is reading a necessary condition as a sufficient one**, and it has a reliable
tell: **you reason from the gate you just touched.** I had landed the face, so the face was the gate
in hand, and *the face serves* became *the case is visible* without a step in between. A second gate
that nobody is currently working on is invisible in exactly the way a second store is (R794) — not
hidden, just not the thing being held.

**And the series is load-bearing, not redundant.** R695 hid eleven PAID VR doors by deriving
visibility from the pool, which is what makes *visible and empty* unreachable rather than merely
discouraged. **A window that cannot open is worth more than a window nobody opens**, and the two
gates in series are what buy that.

## R874 — An empty prior is a state, and the first landing is the only moment it exists

Registered as the form, from the pre-face retention.

**A retention condition that tests the prior for CONTENT will skip the empty prior**, and the empty
prior is the one that carries the fact worth keeping: that the slot was empty, and what it held
instead. `prior && prior.title` read the empty string as *nothing to retain* — the same conflation
R842 drew between ABSENT and PENDING, in a different file and a different direction.

**And the timing makes it unrecoverable rather than merely missing.** The pre-face state exists at
exactly one moment: the first landing. Every later landing has a prior FACE to retain, so the gap is
invisible from the second landing onward — **the only run that could have caught it is the only run
that could have lost it.**

**Nothing was lost here and that was luck.** The marker's bytes had crossed in another artefact for
an unrelated instruction (R861). **A retention that depends on the state having been copied elsewhere
is not a retention**, and a store that discovers its retention worked because of a coincidence should
read that as a failure with a good outcome, not as a pass.

## R875 — A field nobody reads is the field every merge prefers

Cowork's finding, 2026-08-29, registered because **my rows carry them too**: 1,849 fields in the send
arrived by INHERITANCE — carried forward with an item, a role or a template — and were never read at
either store. Its number is quoted as its own (R25); mine is measured below.

**The half that makes it a fault rather than clutter is the dominance test.** Reconciliation between
the stores is field-by-field, and the side a GATE FORCED is the side that exports back (CLAUDE.md,
R23). A field nothing reads can never BE gate-forced, so it never moves, so it agrees on every diff —
and a diff scores agreement as correctness. **The least-scrutinised fields win the most merges, and
they win them for the precise reason that ought to disqualify them.** Stability is being read as
assent. It is R173's camouflage — the confirming number nobody investigates — operating on a store
instead of on an instrument.

**MY SIDE, MEASURED** (`pnpm check:inherited-fields`): 1,227 items, 30 distinct stem keys, 3,398
row-fields. The canonical `stemSchema` validates FIVE key names — `passageRef`, `lineRefs`, `quotes`,
`sentence`, `testedTokens` — and passes every other key through untouched, which is R57 working
exactly as ruled AND is the mechanism by which a field arrives and is never looked at. Three of those
five are present here (757 row-fields); 26 keys on 2,640 row-fields are read somewhere but validated
by no door; one key on one row is neither. **The one is not the finding — the 26 are.** A field the
door does not know is a field the door cannot force, and every one of those 2,640 is a field the
dominance test would prefer.

**AND THE MEASUREMENT FAILED TWICE BEFORE IT REPORTED, BOTH TIMES IN THE SHAPE OF ITS OWN SUBJECT.**
First it printed **0 of 30 read**: invoked through `pnpm --filter @cluecrew/db`, so the cwd was
`packages/db`, every relative source root missed, grep exited non-zero, and a `catch` returned
'absent' — R173's `?? []` inside the check written to count unread fields. Then, repaired, it printed
**29 of 30 read**, which is a saturated proxy: `text`, `code`, `sum`, `question`, `words`, `series`
match any identifier in a monorepo. **The first number was alarming and got investigated; the second
was reassuring and nearly did not.** Only the third — reading the door's own key list — is an
artefact rather than a proxy. Grep for a NAME answers a different question from "is this field read",
and the two agree often enough to hide the difference.

## R876 — A mint quoting a fence a later amendment moved past

`percentage-never-divided-by-hundred` named its carrier as `MC01-FDP-03` option C, value `"2000"`.
The store holds `"£2000"`. The join REFUSED on byte-identity, correctly — and **the cause is neither
store's transcription.** Her own 180th amended those values (*money keys and money options carry
their unit; the nine bare keys amend as a class*) after the population the mint quotes
(`1d7f9cf414f33a0a…`) was fenced, and her 182nd is explicitly fenced against that same digest. **A
fence is a promise about a snapshot, and a later ruling is entitled to move past it** — so the two
facts are both true and the artefacts disagree anyway.

**MY FIRST READING WAS THAT MY EXPORTER HAD STRIPPED THE £, AND I WAS ABOUT TO REPORT IT AS MY
DEFECT.** The send carries 104 `"value": "£…"` occurrences, so no wholesale stripping had happened;
what looked like an emitter bug was a row that had legitimately changed underneath a fence. R834 made
me quick to suspect my own projection, and that priming produced a confident wrong answer in the
opposite direction. Suspecting yourself is not the same as checking.

**THE REFUSAL STANDS EVEN THOUGH THE IDENTITY IS PROVEN.** Four independent declarations agree: the
row id, the label `C`, the option's own retained `_previousValue` byte-identical to the declared
`"2000"`, and the working `25 x 80 = 2000` computing to the option's numeric value. Nothing is
inferred. **And it still refuses**, because landing it means adding retention-matching as a
carrier-selection rule, invented mid-run to turn a red row green — which is R149's fault with better
motivation. The evidence travels with the refusal so she can settle it in one line; the gate does not
settle it on her behalf.

## R877 — What a signature actually covers: pin, verdict, and the fields inside one but not the other

David's scoping, 2026-08-29, recorded on every row signed under it:

- **A PIN asserts IDENTITY over the whole row**, under its named projection.
- **A VERDICT asserts READING over what was actually read.**
- **The INHERITED FIELDS are inside the pin and outside the reading — pinned and unread.**

The three are different scopes and a signature that blurs them claims more than she gave. The pin's
projection here is `{stem, options[{content,isCorrect}], explanation}` with `_`-keys stripped, so it
covers every inherited stem key — the 2,640 row-fields R875 counts are all inside somebody's pin and
none of them are inside anybody's reading. `options[].misconceptionId` is OUTSIDE the projection,
which is why a join can unblock a row without voiding her verification; that is a fact about the
projection and it is ASSERTED per row before each signature, never assumed.

## R878 — A working that names an operation in words has not computed

Her computes-as condition asks whether a carrier's working computes as the entry's behaviour. Two of
seven workings write arithmetic (`15 divided by 3`, `(5 + 3, 4)`) and execute; three name the act in
English (*the largest of 6, 3, 7 and 4*; *digits 6, 4, 0 in descending order*) and execute nothing.
**Those three refuse.** Building an English-phrase-to-operation mapper to land them is R826 exactly —
three signals withdrawn for deciding "does this option execute this error" by inference, every one
measuring something else — and the fact that a mapper's failure mode is a safe refusal does not make
writing one mid-run a good idea. **The narrowness has to be declared rather than discovered**, so the
gate prints what arithmetic it extracted and from which substring on every row (R569), and names the
one line that would land each refusal: a declared expression in the sender's hand.

**AND THE WORKING IS NOT ITSELF HER RULING.** The file says the workings were COMPUTED BY THE SENDER
from her behaviours. So a working cannot supply the human ruling the gate accepts in place of
execution — the entry is hers, the carrier choice is Cowork's, and only the first carries her
authority (R203: where the fact is doubt, the doubt travels with the value).

## R879 — A working supplied by the party naming the entry is not the carrier's own evidence

David's ruling, 2026-08-29, registered from the maths join gate.

**When one party names the entry, names the carrier AND supplies the account of how that carrier
executes the entry, the join has one source wearing three hats.** The working reads as corroboration
and is not: it is the same claim, restated in arithmetic. Executing it tests whether the sender's
arithmetic is internally consistent — never whether the option a child meets executes the error the
entry describes. **The check runs, it passes, and it has not tested the thing its name says.** That
is R173's family — an instrument returning the right shape for the wrong reason — arriving through
the join rather than through a query.

So the carrier's own evidence is the only evidence that separates the two: a working the ITEM states,
authored when the option was written, by somebody who did not know which entry would later claim it.

**AND THE RULING'S STATED PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD HERE, WHICH IS THE HALF WORTH KEEPING** (R880 below).

## R880 — The premise was that two joins landed on carriers stating their own working. None does.

Measured before crossing: **none of the seven named options states a working of its own.** All seven
carry `label` and `value` and nothing else. `distractorWorking` does not exist in this store — not a
column, not a key on any of 4,597 options. `misconceptionExecution` is set on 1,140 options
store-wide and on **0 of 748 MATHS options**.

**So what separated the two joins that landed from the five that refused was EXECUTABILITY, NOT
PROVENANCE.** Both landed on the sender's working; they landed because that working happened to be
written as arithmetic (`15 divided by 3`, `(5 + 3, 4)`) rather than as English. Under R879 the two
rest on exactly the evidence the ruling declines, and the gate that refused five for the right
reason let two through for a reason it did not check. **A gate can be correct on every row it
refuses and still be wrong about what it is measuring.**

The exposure is two joined options (`MC01-FDP-08 C`, `MC01-GEOM-04 D`) and **one signed row**
(`MC01-GEOM-04`, signed because that join unblocked it). **Nothing was unwound.** Applying a ruling
whose stated premise has just been falsified is itself a reading, and the reading belongs to the
party who made the ruling — the same line R867 drew when a gate and a reviewer disagreed.

**THE GENERAL FORM: A PREMISE INSIDE A RULING IS A CLAIM ABOUT THE STORE AND GETS LOOKED UP LIKE ANY
OTHER (R178).** Rules arrive with their reasons attached, the reason contains a fact, and the fact
travels unchecked because it is riding inside an instruction rather than sitting in a field. The
ruling can be right and its premise wrong at the same time — that is this entry — and adopting the
premise silently would have made a measured 0-of-748 into a settled 2-of-7 nobody would re-measure.
Fourth time this month a stated figure needed verifying before use (R866 the eight, R859 the twelve,
R863 the routed claim, now this); the cost each time is one query.

## R881 — The evidence is where the evidence is: the join reads the carrier's working from crossed bytes

David's ruling, 2026-08-29, closing R879/R880.

**`distractorWorking` never crossed this door, and the reader test was right to refuse to widen for
it** — nothing here renders it, and a field no reader consumes is a field this store should not hold
(R601). The fault was one step later: *we do not hold it* became *it does not exist*, and the join
demanded the carrier's evidence in a column that had been deliberately ruled out of existence.
**Requiring evidence in the wrong place is indistinguishable, from inside, from the evidence being
absent.** Cowork holds it on all seven carriers; this store holds it on none; both facts were true
and the conclusion drawn from them was false.

So the join reads the carrier's working from the authoring store's CROSSED BYTES
(`scripts/lib/crossed-carrier-working.ts`), under three properties:
 1. **THE SOURCE IS DERIVED, NEVER PICKED** (R57) — every crossed artefact stating a
    `distractorWorking` is scanned. Naming one file makes the answer depend on which copy somebody
    reached for.
 2. **UNANIMITY REQUIRED, DISAGREEMENT REFUSED** — two copies stating different workings returns
    DISAGREE with every reading and its files. It does not choose. Measured: 12 copies hold all
    seven carriers and agree on every working; they differ only on FDP-03's *value*, where the three
    newest already carry `£2000`. **The mint quoted an older copy than its own store's current
    bytes** — which is R876's fence, seen from the sending side.
 3. **THE KEYS PRINTED BEFORE THE VALUES** (R568). The first scan of these files looked for `id`
    where the shape says `itemId`, found nothing across 196 items, and reported 0 carriers — a
    failed read wearing the exact shape of the true absence it was sent to check. **Third time in
    this thread that a wrong key name produced a confident zero**, and the only reason it did not
    stand was that the digest was known-good, so the zero was impossible rather than merely wrong.

**THE TWO LANDED JOINS SURVIVE THE RE-FOUNDING, AND THAT IS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED.** The gate
refuses an already-tagged option before it computes, so re-running it could never answer R880's open
question; `refound-joins-on-carrier-evidence.ts` answers it without writing anything. `15 / 3 = 5`
and `5 + 3 = 8 → (8, 4)` both verify on the carrier's own working. Carrier and sender agree on all
seven — **an outcome, not evidence that the design held** (R62). The divergence R879 guards against
did not happen this time; the guard is not thereby unnecessary.

**AND THE EXTRACTOR NEEDED A THIRD FORM, WHICH THE FIXTURE CAUGHT RATHER THAN THE ROWS.** The
carriers' idiom is the ASSERTION (`80 x 25 = 2000`), the sender's was BARE (`15 divided by 3`) and
TUPLE (`(5 + 3, 4)`). Replacing bare with assertion silently dropped a capability, and the carried
fixture failed on the case the change removed — not on a row, not in a report, in the instrument's
own must-catch list. **The assertion form is WEAKER and it says so at its definition**: it checks the
arithmetic is internally correct and that its result appears AMONG the option's components, which on
`(8, 4)` is not reproduction. Said at the definition rather than left to be discovered (R591).

Refusals after the re-founding, now on the carrier's own evidence: `biggest number = 7`,
`6,4,0 = 640`, `put 6 first, then 0,4 -> 604` state no arithmetic. **The refusal is the same and its
footing is not** — three rows previously refused on the sender's silence are now refused on the
carrier's own, which is the only version of that refusal that means anything.

Still open and not decided here: FDP-03 C, where the carrier's working verifies and only the mint's
stale declared value blocks it; and FDP-08 D, where the conditional's antecedent — *the store's
declared gap prose* — now EXISTS (`15 / (1/4) = 60`) and whether it agrees with the sender's account
is a reading. **Both are hers.** Nothing was unwound, nothing was landed.

## R882 — Agreement between two sources is an outcome; it is never evidence the separation held

Carrier evidence and sender evidence agreed on all seven named joins. **That is a fact about these
seven rows and says nothing whatever about whether reading the sender's working would have been
safe.** R879 exists because one party naming the entry, the carrier and the working is one claim
wearing three hats; the hats did not come apart this time.

**The reasoning that must not be allowed to run is: "we changed the evidence source and every verdict
stayed the same, so the source did not matter."** It is R62's finding in a different clothing — zero
divergence there was also an outcome, and the coupling that produced it was live, unguarded and
exercised the same day. Here the sender's workings happened to be honest transcriptions of the
carriers'. A sender who had computed a working FROM the entry rather than from the item would have
produced exactly the same agreement rate on rows where the entry is correct, and a silent
disagreement on precisely the rows where it is not — **the failure mode is invisible in the
aggregate and concentrated in the cases that matter.**

**So the number to report is not the agreement rate; it is which source was consulted.** An artefact
saying *carrier and sender agree, 7 of 7* invites the reader to conclude the distinction is
academic. It says instead which evidence counted, per row, and records the other as provenance.

## R883 — A structural walker has R568's failure mode and none of R568's guard

A scan of the crossed artefacts selected rows by SHAPE — `'id' in o && Array.isArray(o.options)` —
where the files say `itemId`. It matched nothing across 196 items and reported **0 carriers holding
a working**, which is the precise answer the scan had been written to test for. Third confident zero
from a wrong key name in this thread (R568's `hintCore`, R80's moved `lineRefs`, now this).

**R568 does not reach it.** That rule guards a delivery reading a NAMED field: print the keys
present, throw when a requested name is on no row. A structural walker asks no name — it asks a
shape — so there is no requested name to check and nothing throws. **The predicate that selects the
rows has the same failure mode as the predicate that reads the fields, and only one of them was
guarded.** So: any walker selecting rows by key-shape prints the keys it saw at each level and
REFUSES on an empty selection from a non-empty file, exactly as a named read refuses a name on no
row (`crossedOptionKeys()`, and the throw in `sources()`).

**AND THE HALF WORTH KEEPING IS WHY IT DID NOT STAND.** Not vigilance, and not the output — a true
zero and this zero are byte-identical downstream. It fell because an INDEPENDENT INVARIANT made it
impossible: the file's digest was known-good and its provenance known, so *196 items, 0 with the
field* was not a surprising result but a contradiction. **The guard against a wrong-key zero is
holding a second fact that the wrong answer violates**, not reading more carefully. Where no such
fact exists, the code has to manufacture one, which is all `requirePopulation`, `readFieldsByName`
and `declareMayBeEmpty` have ever been. A zero that is merely *unexpected* gets argued with; a zero
that is *impossible* gets investigated.

## R884 — A carried fixture's first live catch, and what it caught: a removed capability, not an added bug

Wiring R881 replaced the extractor's bare-arithmetic branch with the carriers' assertion idiom
(`80 x 25 = 2000`). The change was correct for every carrier and it **silently dropped the ability to
read a bare expression** (`15 divided by 3`). The carried fixture failed on the must-catch case the
change removed — in the instrument, before a single row was read, with the run refusing to print
findings at all.

**Nothing in the corpus would have caught it.** The three word-workings refuse either way; the two
landed options short-circuit on `already tagged` before any arithmetic runs; no remaining row uses
the bare form. **A removed capability produces no wrong answer — it produces no answer, on inputs
that have stopped arriving.** That is why it is invisible to every check that reads output: R87's
silent no-op and R61's absent population are the same shape, and this is the first of the family
that a fixture caught rather than a person noticing afterwards.

**So a fixture is the instrument's memory of what it used to be able to do**, and that is a different
thing from a test of what it currently does. The must-catch list is the only place the bare form
still existed. R725 queued fixtures on the argument that a check should earn one before its next
emission crosses; the argument was about trusting findings. **This is the stronger reason: without
the fixture, the capability would have gone and the diff would have looked like a clean improvement**
— fourteen carried cases now, and the one that fired was the one nobody would have thought to re-add.

## R885 — The condition tests that the working DETERMINES the value; the name said computes

Annie's 192nd, 2026-08-29. **Computes-as was never about arithmetic.** Her words: *the stated act,
run on the item's own material, produces exactly this value and no other.* Long division qualifies;
so does selection; so does ordering. What the condition refuses is GESTURE — a working that makes its
value plausible rather than inevitable.

**THE NAME SAID COMPUTES AND THE TEST MEANT DETERMINES**, which is R871's `maxLongWords` fault
landing on the reviewer's own condition rather than on our instrument. She named it before it cost
anyone a wrong argument; three joins were refused on it first. So `scripts/lib/determination.ts` is
named for what it tests and `determines()` is the only entry point.

**A CLOSED SET OF ACTS, NOT AN INTERPRETER.** Widening to "any stated act" is precisely where R826's
inference creeps back, so each act is NAMED, recognised by a declared vocabulary, and EXECUTED over
the item's own material: `arithmetic`, `selection` (largest/smallest over the numbers the stem
states), `permutation` (a stated order of the item's digits, concatenated). A working matching none
is refused. The act that matched and the material it ran on travel on every result (R569).

**"AND NO OTHER" IS HALF THE TEST AND IT IS WHERE THE TEETH ARE.** A tied selection determines
nothing even when it names the right value; a permutation whose digits are not the item's determines
some other item's answer. Both are carried as must-be-clean fixture cases, because both would
otherwise pass as "the act produced the option".

## R886 — A join's declared value re-derives against the carrier's current bytes at landing

Annie's 192nd §2, on her own artefact: **she computed the join from a population snapshot and the
money-units class landed after the cut**, so her file quoted `2000` where the store rightly carries
`£2000`. Born-stale (R876) arriving on the reviewer's side of the exchange. The repair is the
standing rule applied to joins — the mechanism and the working unchanged, the number keeping its
deliberate wrongness with its unit attached.

**RE-DERIVATION CORROBORATES; IT DOES NOT BELIEVE.** Identity anchors on the label, and a declared
value matching neither the carrier's current bytes NOR its retained prior names something that
carrier has never been — that refuses. Without the corroboration, "re-derive" degrades to "believe
whichever option the label points at", which is R865's stretch by another route. Here the retained
`_previousValue` is byte-identical to her declaration, so the re-derivation is evidenced rather than
assumed, and the artefact records declared, re-derived, and what corroborated it.

## R887 — A fixture case a ruling invalidates is retired in the commit that implements the ruling

Two carried cases asserted that `the largest of 6, 3, 7 and 4` and `digits 6, 4, 0 in descending
order` must NOT verify. **They were correct while the condition was read as arithmetic and R885 makes
them wrong.** A stale must-be-clean case is an instrument enforcing a superseded rule: it fails
loudly on the now-correct behaviour, and the failure looks exactly like a regression.

So the retirement happens in the same commit as the ruling, in the file, with the reason written
where the cases were — never by quietly deleting them and never by leaving them to fail. **A fixture
is the instrument's memory (R884), and a memory nobody curates becomes a rule nobody voted for.**

## R888 — Which projection a pin was taken under is DISCOVERED, never declared

`sign-joins-unblocked.ts` named one projection — retention EXCLUDED — and asserted it in every
signature's `method`. **Every maths pin was in fact taken with retention INCLUDED.**

**It passed anyway on three rows.** A row carrying no `_`-key hashes identically under both
projections, so the claim was untestable exactly where it was false and self-confirming everywhere
else. Three signatures landed carrying a method string that names a projection which was not the one
used; the verification behind them was sound, and the record of it was not.

**The one row that could expose it did, and the exposure did not look like a projection fault.**
`MC01-FDP-03` carries `_previousValue`, so the two projections diverge on it — and the refusal read
*the row does not recompute to her pin*, which is the wording for a content problem. R859 said a
digest is comparable only under the projection it was made with; **this is the next step — you do not
get to declare which that was.** Both are now computed, the pin is matched against both, and the
signature records WHICH, noting when the two are indistinguishable on that row.

The three earlier signatures were corrected by ADDING a correcting event, not by rewriting the
originals: a record is corrected by adding to it. And the fixture now carries the discriminating
pair — retention present (projections differ) and retention absent (projections agree) — because the
second case is the reason the first went unnoticed.

## R889 — A check that agrees with itself wherever it cannot be tested is not a check

The full-reach form of R888, and the one to carry forward.

**A check asserts a claim, and its population splits in two: rows where the claim is TESTABLE, and
rows where it is DEGENERATE — where both branches of the claim give the same answer.** On a
degenerate row the check passes no matter which branch is true. It is not a weak test there; it is
NO test, and it is indistinguishable in the output from a strong one. **The degenerate rows do not
merely fail to help — they manufacture the confidence that stops anyone looking.** Three signatures
carried a false statement about how they were verified, and three green rows are why nobody asked.

**SO EVERY CHECK REPORTS ITS DISCRIMINATING DENOMINATOR: on how many rows could this claim have been
FALSIFIED?** Not how many rows were screened (R60) — how many could have said no.
`THE_DISCRIMINATING_DENOMINATOR` in `sign-joins-unblocked.ts` is the shape: rows compared, rows where
the branches differ, rows where the claim is degenerate, and the ids of the discriminating ones. **A
discriminating count of zero is R61's absent population one level down** — the rows are there, the
check ran, and the claim was tested on nothing. It must print as UNVERIFIED, never as a pass.

**AND THE ONE ROW THAT COULD FALSIFY IT WAS THE ONE THAT DID.** `MC01-FDP-03` is the only maths row
carrying retention, so it is the only row on which the two projections diverge — and it is the only
row that refused. That is not luck; it is the definition. **A single discriminating row outweighs the
entire agreeing remainder, and the remainder's size is what makes it feel otherwise.**

**THE FALSIFICATION ARRIVED WEARING THE WRONG LABEL, WHICH IS WHY THIS NEEDS A MECHANISM AND NOT
VIGILANCE.** The refusal read *the row does not recompute to her pin* — the wording for a content
fault, on a signed row, pointing at the reviewer's own amendment. Every instinct it triggers is to
investigate the DATA. The instrument was wrong, the data was fine, and nothing in the message could
have told them apart. Sibling to R173 (right answer, wrong reason) and R149 (the fault that looks
like content and is the instrument), and the discriminating denominator is the first guard here that
would have caught it BEFORE the row did.

## R890 — Widening a condition safely: a closed set of named acts, proved by its accidents

R885 widened *computes-as* from arithmetic to determination — from one mechanical test to **any
stated act**. That is the most dangerous shape of change available here, because "any stated act" is
an invitation to infer, and R826 withdrew three signals for exactly that. The form that survives it:

1. **THE SET IS CLOSED AND EACH ACT IS NAMED.** `arithmetic`, `selection`, `permutation`. Not a
   parser for English, a vocabulary for three procedures.
2. **EACH ACT RUNS ON THE SUBJECT'S OWN MATERIAL** — the numbers and digits the item itself states,
   never material supplied by the party making the claim (R879).
3. **NON-RECOGNITION REFUSES.** A working matching no act is gesture. The failure direction is
   refusal, so a widening cannot silently admit more than it names.
4. **THE ACT AND THE MATERIAL TRAVEL ON THE RESULT** (R569), because a verdict whose procedure the
   reader cannot see is a verdict taken on trust.

**AND THE TWO MUST-BE-CLEAN CASES ARE WHAT MAKE IT A TEST OF DETERMINATION RATHER THAN OF
PRODUCTION.** A TIED SELECTION — *largest of [7, 7]* — produces the right value and determines
nothing. An UNGROUNDED PERMUTATION — digits that are not the item's, concatenated — produces the
right value and determines some other item's answer. **Both would pass a check that asked "does the
act produce the option", and both must fail, because the condition is "produces exactly this value
AND NO OTHER".**

**The transferable half: for any "does X produce Y" check, the must-be-clean cases are the ones where
X produces Y BY ACCIDENT** — ties, coincidences, ungrounded inputs, degenerate arguments. Without
them a closed set of acts is a value-matcher wearing an act's name, and it will agree with every
correct row and every lucky one alike. Those cases are also the ones nobody writes unprompted, since
they require imagining the check succeeding for the wrong reason — which is the whole skill.

## R891 — A tag whose every member sits where the rival rules coincide is a taxonomy without its negative control

Annie's 193rd §3, and she calls it the largest thing in the file. **Every carrier of the unit-fraction
tag sits on a fraction where the two rival rules give the same answer, and twenty-six discriminating
fractions rode in the same send untagged.** A tag like that has never been tested against its rival:
every member confirms it, none could have refused it, and the confirmation is worth nothing.

**This is R889 at the level of DIAGNOSIS rather than of code.** A check that agrees with itself
wherever it cannot be tested is not a check; a tag whose members all sit on the coincidence set is
not a diagnosis — **it names a family and is recorded as naming a member.** The discriminating
denominator of the whole tag is zero.

The repair is hers and it is one authored item: **a fraction of the form 2/5, where the complement
and the unit fraction part company and a child's answer says which rule she runs.** Until it exists
the tag cannot distinguish what it claims to distinguish, and the honest instrument in the meantime
is a hint that survives either reading (R892).

## R892 — On this fraction the arithmetic does not decide, so the join says so

The join of `MC01-FDP-08` D lands on her ruling and **NOT on determination**, and the artefact
records that distinction rather than smoothing it. `15 × 4 = 60` (the bottom used alone) and
`15 ÷ (1 − 3/4) = 60` (the complement) are the same number, because on a fraction of the form
(b−1)/b the complement equals the unit fraction by coincidence. **The determination check runs, and
it verifies equally well for the rule she refused** — so recording this join as "verified" would be a
true-looking sentence about a test that separated nothing.

Her three grounds are outside the arithmetic: the item's architecture pairs C and D as one act in two
halves; the stem invites no complement because no remainder is in view; and *uses the complement*
describes the VALUE 1/4 rather than a route a child took to it — the letter-count class, where the
flagNote described the coincidence and the authoredValue described the act.

**HER QUALIFIER TRAVELS WITH THE JOIN, IN HER WORDS: *that is a weaker sentence than a computed join
and it is the true one*.** Without it, this row reads identically to the six that computed and the
reader has no way back to the difference (R203). **A store that can only record "verified" will
record "verified" for everything it lands**, which is how a weaker basis becomes invisible one row at
a time.

And the hint amended for the same reason. The replaced wording ASSERTED the mechanism — *only one
part of the fraction was used* — which lies to a complement child if one exists; the authored
wording *the dividing was not done by the fraction in the question* is true under both readings and
still names the fault rather than the key. R586's assert-or-describe, applied to a population that
has not been measured yet.

## R893 — Two fields on one row answering the same question opposite ways

Annie's 193rd §5, the one-column fault's last costume. `flagNote` described the coincidence and
`authoredValue` described the act; **both were true of the same option and they answered the same
question differently, with nothing on the row saying which governed.** A reader takes whichever they
open first, and neither is wrong, so nothing ever surfaces the conflict.

**Fields that answer the same question either agree, or the row names which is authoritative.** This
is R608's split-decision fault (a directive and its reason wearing one name) turned the other way
round: there the two fields were one decision and neither sorted; here they are two decisions and
neither yields. Same remedy — **name the authority at the field's definition**, not one field over
and not in prose.

**And the companion line, from the store's own conduct: a verdict reached from a subset of the
evidence, published without naming the subset, is worse than no verdict, because it looks settled.**
Her words, registered from this store reopening its own agreement on exactly that ground. It is
R889's shape stated as a duty rather than as a mechanism: naming the subset is what lets a reader
compute the discriminating denominator you did not.

## R894 — A store that can only record "verified" will record "verified" for everything it lands

The form behind R892, and it is about the VOCABULARY OF VERDICTS rather than about one join.

**A check that runs and separates nothing has not verified anything, and the artefact must be able to
say so.** On `MC01-FDP-08` D the determination check ran, returned true, and decided nothing: the two
rival rules coincide on that fraction, so the check verifies equally well for the reading the
reviewer refused. Recording it as *verified* would have been a true sentence about a test that
distinguished nothing — the R173 family, arriving in the verdict rather than in the measurement.

**THREE THINGS TOGETHER, AND NONE OF THEM SUFFICES ALONE:**
 1. **The check still runs.** Skipping it because a ruling covers the row throws away the fact that
    the arithmetic was consistent, and leaves nobody able to tell "not computed" from "not checked".
 2. **The artefact records that it decided nothing**, and why — `NOT_LANDED_ON_COMPUTATION: true`
    beside `whatTheComputationSAYS` and `andWHYTHATDOESNOTDECIDE`. A verdict without its basis is a
    name with no guard on it (R25).
 3. **The qualifier travels with the join**, in the reviewer's words rather than paraphrased: *that
    is a weaker sentence than a computed join and it is the true one.* R203 — where the fact is
    doubt, the doubt goes in the same value, not one field over.

**THE FAILURE MODE IS INSTITUTIONAL, NOT TECHNICAL.** A store whose verdict vocabulary has one word
will use that word for the strong rows and the weak ones alike, and no reader will ever be able to
sort them again — not because anything was hidden, but because the distinction was never expressible.
**Six joins here computed and one did not, and after the fact only the artefact can tell you which.**
So the verdict set carries at least: DETERMINED (the act separates this option from the
alternatives), RULED (a reviewer decided on grounds outside the check, which ran and separated
nothing), and REFUSED. A basis that cannot be named will be recorded as the nearest basis that can.

**And the same discipline reaches an unwind.** Retagging `MC01-FDP-08` D would write a new
`misconceptionId` and, unless the ruling basis is carried onto the new attribution event verbatim,
would leave D looking exactly like the six that computed. **A weaker basis is lost by ordinary
maintenance, not by anybody deciding to drop it** — which is why the retirement impact report names
it as the one thing that would go silently.

## R895 — A qualifier belongs to a JOIN, not to an ENTRY, and survives a retag intact

Annie's 194th finding, and this store had already named it as the thing that would go missing.

`MC01-FDP-08` D joined on a ruling rather than a computation (R892), and the qualifier saying so
lived on the join's attribution event. **Retiring the entry retags the option, which writes a new
`misconceptionId` — and a retag that does not carry the qualifier forward leaves D indistinguishable
from the six joins that computed.** Nobody would have decided to drop it. Ordinary maintenance would
have.

**THE CARRY IS VERBATIM, FROM THE EVENT THAT HOLDS IT, NEVER RE-AUTHORED.** Re-typing a qualifier
during a move is a second wording under one id (R598), and the wording is the reviewer's. The new
event quotes the original `method` and `note` in full and says it is quoting; the assertion that the
carry is intact is CHECKED after the write, not assumed.

**The general shape: provenance attaches at the grain of the DECISION, not at the grain of the
record that happens to hold it.** A basis recorded on an entry dies with the entry; a basis recorded
on the join survives every move of the entry, because the join is what the basis is about. Anything
that can be relocated — a tag, an id, a carrier — must be asked, before it moves, what qualifiers
are riding on it. The impact report is that question in mechanical form (R894), and this is the case
where asking it in advance is the only reason the answer was available afterwards.

## R896 — The register's own words outlast every paraphrase of them

Her 194th §2, and it closes the excursion. **The gap was declared against a misremembered quotation
of an entry she had approved herself**, in her 134th, by reference under the head declaration.
`maths-75` was cited as *using only the numerator*; its actual bytes name the numerator OR the
denominator used alone, and give as its denominator example *15 divided by 3/4 = 5* — which is the
exact item and the exact option value that the mint was created to diagnose.

**Every paraphrase in this excursion was wrong somewhere and the bytes never were.** Mine (the
premise about carriers stating their own workings, R880), hers (the quotation the gap was declared
on), and the desk's (the eight-versus-eleven attribution, R866). Three parties, three paraphrases,
three faults — and in each case the repair was the same act: read the value, not the account of it
(R25). **A quotation with an ellipsis is not bytes**, and neither is a summary, a recollection, or a
count carried forward from a message.

**AND THE COROLLARY THAT COST THE MOST HERE: a rejection that names no register version becomes
unreadable the day the register changes.** Option C's `flagNote` rejects an id that was retired into
another entry, so it is dated rather than judged — survival, not judgement. A field asserting a
negative about the library must say which library it was true of, or it decays into a contradiction
nobody can adjudicate and everybody must route around.

## R897 — A figure that enumerates a rule's membership goes stale the moment a ruling changes it

The closing report defined *joined* as **tagged with one of these six ids** — an enumeration of who
was a member on the day it was written, not of the property that made them members. It was correct
for a week. It printed `joins 5 of 7` the instant `fraction-part-used-alone` retired, because two
carriers had moved to the replacement and the enumeration had no way to know a ruling had happened.

**The count still computed, still printed, and still looked like a measurement.** That is R180's
rot, and the specific mechanism worth naming: **a definition by enumeration is a snapshot of a rule's
output wearing the rule's name.** Every ruling that moves membership — a retirement, a merge, a
rename, a re-tier — invalidates it silently, and the artefact goes on reporting with confidence
about a population that has moved underneath it. **Both stores would have read 5 of 7 as two joins
lost.**

**AND THE OVER-CORRECTION IS THE SECOND HALF, BECAUSE IT IS THE PREDICTABLE ONE.** The repair
instinct is to widen the enumeration — add the replacement id — which swept `maths-75`'s eleven
pre-existing carriers into the count and printed **18 of 7**. That is R591 turned on our own report:
a figure claiming a population wider than the thing behind it. **The correction was larger than the
error and in the same direction of carelessness**, and it arrived while I was already looking
straight at the number.

**The repair is to define the population by what made it one** — here, the options the mint file
NAMED — and let membership FOLLOW rulings: a named carrier is joined when it carries its entry or the
entry that entry retired into. That survives a retirement without inflating, because nothing about it
is a list.

**THE GUARD IS ARITHMETIC AND IT COSTS NOTHING: a numerator may not exceed its own denominator.**
`18 of 7` is impossible on its face and printed without complaint, which is the whole lesson in one
line — the report had no opinion about its own coherence. `emit-maths-closing-report.ts` now throws
on it, with the message pointing at the membership rule rather than at the number, because the number
is never the thing to fix.

## R898 — The maths district publishes: 178 live, nine held by a mechanism, window zero

David's ruling, 2026-08-30, executed in one transaction on the case-en-06 shape.

**A CORRECTION WALKED RATHER THAN ADOPTED.** The instruction said the 178 move *DRAFT to LIVE*.
They were **REVIEWED**; the nine that stay are the DRAFT ones. The move is REVIEWED → LIVE. Every
figure here was derived from the rows at the moment of publication and none was carried forward from
the instruction — which is the only reason that discrepancy surfaced rather than being reproduced in
the artefact (R896).

**EIGHT ASSERTIONS RAN BEFORE THE WRITE, ANY FAILURE REFUSING THE WHOLE RUN**: 178 of 178 signatures
over pins that recompute under their own projection (both projections tried, per R888); 7 of 7 joins
standing; the face serving; **the held set identical to the set `publishBlockers` computes** — so no
row is held by hand and none caught by accident; 178 + 9 = 187; nothing held from serving; every row
already in the practice pool. A partial publication is the half-applied-import fault with children on
the other end of it.

**SIX ROWS SERVE CHILDREN CARRYING A LIVE GATE FAULT, AND THE ARTEFACT SAYS SO IN THOSE WORDS.**
Each of the six over-cap stems carries a per-row reviewer disposition — *the sixteen-word cap binds
hints, so an over-cap stem stands* — recorded before the row was signed. The gate still reports them
because the gate was deliberately not changed. **Both authorities agree and the only dissent is the
gate, which holds neither** (R867), so they publish NAMED rather than silently exempted, and the
question the register deferred stays open: whether the sixteen-word cap should bind an item stem at
all. **The house rule is never exempt a scanner hit — reword it; six rows are now live against it on
a reviewer's ruling, and that sentence is in the publication artefact rather than in a footnote.**

**THE WINDOW IS ZERO AND STRUCTURALLY SO.** The face and the pool landed in the same act, and
`servableCaseIds` derives visibility from the pool at request time, so *visible and empty* is
unreachable rather than merely unobserved (R873/R695). Verified independently after the write by
reading the store rather than the artefact: 178 LIVE+PRACTICE, `case-maths-01` in the servable set,
17 of 28 cases servable, 0 visible-and-empty.

**THE BLAST RADIUS WAS WALKED FROM THE ROWS**, not assumed to be one case: every case whose primary
or mapped question type appears among the newly-live rows was enumerated from the case table. The
district's paid door now opens onto 178 items across seven question types.

Nine rows remain DRAFT with 15 untagged distractors, named per row with their causes on the
artefact. **Open at 178 with the nine held.**

## R899 — A withdrawal recorded as an event and never executed as a removal

**Six rows served children on bytes from a send their author had withdrawn.** Each carried, on its
own row, an event reading *"the 196-row send was WITHDRAWN by the authoring store; this id is not in
the replacement send. **The row is removed before anything publishes.**"* The removal never happened.
The rows went marker → SIGNED → PUBLISHED, and the instruction sat on each one the whole way.

**THE MARKER IS INDISTINGUISHABLE, DOWNSTREAM, FROM NO WITHDRAWAL AT ALL.** It is prose in a
`method` field. Nothing reads it, so nothing enforces it — R601 exactly: *a decision nothing reads is
not a decision*, arriving on the most consequential field in the district. The event was written to
be a control and functioned as a note.

**AND THE PUBLICATION'S EIGHT ASSERTIONS WERE ALL SOUND.** Signatures, pins recomputing under their
own projection, joins standing, the face serving, the held set matching the mechanism, the arithmetic
closing, nothing held from serving, every row in the practice pool. **Not one asked which SEND a row
came from.** A complete set of correct assertions about the wrong axis reads exactly like a complete
set of assertions — which is R889 wearing its most expensive costume: every green was real, and the
question that mattered was never put.

**THE COLUMNS COULD NOT HAVE ANSWERED IT EITHER.** `sourcedFrom`, `importDoorFix` and
`draftingMethod` are null on all 187. The district has no per-row record of its own provenance;
what exists lives in `AttributionEvent`, which no gate consults. **The first place I looked returned
"no provenance anywhere" and that was true of the columns and false of the store** — R568's fault
one level up, where the right question asked of the wrong table gives a clean, wrong answer.

`pnpm check:withdrawn-serving` is the missing assertion, standing alone: any row marked by a
withdrawal and serving must carry a LATER AUTHORITY reaching it, and the check prints that authority
per id. **Six of the ten marked-and-live rows had none and came out** (LIVE → REVIEWED, not deleted —
signature, bytes and events intact, reinstatable in one statement). Four stay and the reason is on
the record: `MC01-CALC-01` and `MC01-CALC-05` were re-pinned against the amended source
`4bab53bba515e606` with bytes verified identical to the replacement; `MC04-FDP-04` and `MC05-FDP-01`
were restored on her explicit ruling — *the absence recorded earlier was false and is withdrawn.*
**A row with a later authority is not a withdrawn-send row; a row with none is**, and that
distinction is the whole content of the check.

**A SEPARATE FALSE NOTE, FOUND WHILE ANSWERING.** The restore events on `MC04-FDP-04` and
`MC05-FDP-01` state: *the unchosen variant is recorded on the row and is NOT discarded.* Both stems
carry exactly one key, `text`; `_stemCollisionResolved` is absent on all 187. **The note asserts a
retention that does not exist.** The rows serve the variant she read — attested by her ruling and by
a signature over a pin that recomputes — but from the row you cannot tell a choice was made, which is
precisely what the note promises you can. R872's lesson unlearned in a neighbouring file: a retention
claimed in prose and not written is worse than no retention, because it stops anyone looking.

## R900 — The note was right and the row caught up

The restore events on `MC04-FDP-04` and `MC05-FDP-01` said *the unchosen variant is recorded on the
row and is NOT discarded*. It was not. **The repair is to write the retention, not to correct the
note** — the note described the right behaviour, and a store that fixes the description instead of
the behaviour has chosen the cheaper of two repairs and recorded it as if it were the other one.

The unchosen variants came from **Cowork's crossed bytes**, never re-authored here — this store does
not author item content, and a retention invented locally would be a second wording under one id
(R598). The chosen variant was asserted byte-identical to what the row already serves BEFORE
anything was written: if the store and the sends disagreed about which variant is live, that is a
different and larger fault, and it refuses rather than papering over it.

**THE SIGNATURE SURVIVES BY DESIGN AND WAS ASSERTED ANYWAY.** Both pins are under the
retention-EXCLUDED projection, which strips `_`-keys, so a retention key cannot move them — **which
is precisely what R858 stripped retention FOR**, working here on its first real test rather than
being trusted. The excluded hash is computed before and after inside the transaction, and anything
but equality rolls back.

## R901 — Send history is a property of the row, not a memory of the conversation

Annie's ruling, 2026-08-30, after six rows served children on bytes from a withdrawn send.

**The withdrawal was recorded as prose in an `AttributionEvent` and nothing read it** (R899).
Answering *which of the 187 came from the withdrawn send* took a conversation, four queries against
a table no gate consults, and one wrong start — the provenance COLUMNS (`sourcedFrom`,
`importDoorFix`, `draftingMethod`) are null on all 187, so the first honest answer was "there is no
provenance anywhere", true of the columns and false of the store. **Provenance answerable only by
conversation is provenance that will be wrong the next time nobody asks.**

`Item.sendHistory` now carries, per row, every crossed send holding that id with its digest, row
count and ROLE, plus whether the row is in the withdrawn send and absent from the replacement. It
is DERIVED by scanning the sends (R57) and sits OUTSIDE the pin projection, so recording provenance
cannot falsify a signature — asserted per row inside the transaction.

**THE ROLES HAD TO BE DERIVED FROM MEMBERSHIP, AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT WAS WORTHLESS.** Marking a send
withdrawn because it CONTAINS the withdrawn ids matched every superset and reported **187 of 187**
rows in a withdrawn send — R591's wider-population fault, third instance this week, and this one
would have made the new column useless on the day it landed. The roles that mean something are
defined by what a send OMITS: the replacement omits every marked id; the withdrawn send carries them.
**And one artefact needed a role of its own** — `1d7f9cf4…` is this store's own export of the same
196-row membership, the population Annie content-verified. Calling it a withdrawn send would have
been false, and it is exactly why her 182nd covers rows later withdrawn and why restoring two of
them was sound.

**THE CONFIRMATION WORTH HAVING: the column agrees with the events.** 16 rows are in the withdrawn
send and not the replacement; 16 rows carry the withdrawal marker and are still in the store. Two
derivations from independent sources — the send files and the attribution log — landing on the same
membership. **That is the only kind of agreement this register treats as evidence** (R882): not one
instrument agreeing with itself, but two that could have disagreed.

## R902 — A role is defined by what it OMITS; containment matches every superset

David's ruling, 2026-08-30, from the send-history build.

**A send is the withdrawn one because of what it LEAVES OUT of the replacement, never because of
what it holds.** The first classifier asked *does this artefact contain the withdrawn ids* — and
every superset contains them. It put 26 artefacts in one class and reported **187 of 187** rows as
appearing in a withdrawn send, which is not a finding; it is a classifier with no discriminating
power reporting as confidently as one that has.

**THE MECHANISM IS MONOTONICITY, AND IT IS WHY THIS FAILS SILENTLY AS A CORPUS GROWS.** A
containment predicate is monotone increasing in the data: adding rows to an artefact can only make
it match MORE, never less. So a containment-based role classifier's false positives rise with the
size of the corpus, and nothing in its output changes shape as that happens — it goes on returning
a clean list that quietly becomes the whole population. **An omission predicate is monotone in the
opposite direction**: adding data can only make it fail, so it errs toward refusing to classify
rather than toward classifying everything. **Where a role must be bounded, define it by absence.**

**THE SMELL IS CHEAP AND MECHANICAL: a role matching the entire population is a failure, not a
result.** `attach-send-history.ts` now throws on it. That is R889's discriminating denominator
turned from verification to classification — the question is not how many artefacts a role matched
but how many it could have EXCLUDED, and a role that excludes nothing has been tested against
nothing.

**AND THE THIRD CLASS THE OMISSION TEST MADE VISIBLE.** Defining the roles by absence forced a
distinction containment had hidden entirely: `1d7f9cf4…` carries the withdrawn ids and is not a send
at all — it is this store's own export of the same 196-row membership, the population the reviewer
content-verified. Under containment it was a withdrawn send; under omission it needed a role of its
own, and that role is the reason her verification legitimately covers rows that were later
withdrawn. **A test too coarse to separate two things will not report that it merged them** — it
reports the merged class as a fact, and the distinction is only recovered by someone asking why a
count looks too round.

## R903 — A withdrawal keys on SUBSTANCE, and the receiving door refuses to arm before it can reproduce one

Cowork's withdrawal notice, 2026-08-30, crossed as an ACT addressed to this store — 31 substances of
the 196-row send, six superseded by current bytes and twenty-five with no replacement anywhere.

**THE KEY IS SUBSTANCE AND NEVER ID**, in their words: *MC04-FDP-04 appears below and ALSO exists in
a variant this notice does not touch. A door keying on the id would refuse the repair along with the
fault.* Substance is the stem, the SORTED set of option values, the key, solution, solutionValue and
solutionKind — option order, labels and enrichment deducted, because a shuffle is not a different
question and an unfinished copy is not a different one either. `packages/core/src/item-identity.ts`
implements it; the notice is retained git-tracked at `content/withdrawals/` so the standing
withdrawal is an artefact the door READS rather than a message somebody remembers (R899's whole
lesson).

**THE DOOR IS BUILT AND CORRECTLY REFUSES TO ARM.** It reproduced ZERO of the 31 declared digests
from any bytes this store holds, across sixteen candidate encodings of their six fields. The notice
names the FIELDS and not the SERIALISATION. **Two explanations remain confounded and this store
cannot separate them**: this encoding differs from theirs, or these rows genuinely differ from every
substance named. So it screens nothing and exits non-zero saying why — **a matcher that matches
nothing reports exactly what a clean population reports**, and shipping it green would have been the
ninth instance of the fault this register exists to record. One line unblocks it: their `substance()`
implementation, or one worked example — the input string that hashes to a declared digest.

**AND THE QUESTION DID NOT NEED THE DIGEST.** Their marked inference was that six ids might be
serving pre-amendment money bytes. Refuted by READING: all six carry the united form in the stem and
in every option value. **A verdict blocked on an unbuildable instrument was answerable from the bytes
the whole time** — the digest was the general mechanism and the question was specific, and reaching
for the mechanism first would have delayed a one-line answer indefinitely.

**THE FINDING THAT CAME BACK THE OTHER WAY.** Their CURRENT send `744b3fc8ab16` still carries the
BARE money form in the STEM on all six, while carrying the united form in the option values — the
money amendment reached their values and not their stems. **So their `replacementSubstanceSha256`
values describe rows with pre-amendment stems**, and these six match neither the withdrawn substance
nor the declared replacement: they are a third state, and it is the amended one. Reported as an
observation, not a ruling — which stem form is right is not this store's call — because a replacement
that is itself pre-amendment is a thing the sender wants to know before anybody lifts on it.

## R904 — Armed on evidence: the serialisation nobody would guess, and the ambiguity JSON.parse destroys

Cowork crossed the substance spec with **all thirty-one worked input strings**, not the one example
asked for, on the stated ground that *a door that can check every declared digest ARMS ON EVIDENCE
RATHER THAN ON TRUST*. `check:withdrawn-substance` now carries three canaries and screens nothing
unless all pass: their probe reproduces as a STRING and a digest; 37 of 37 declared digests recompute
from the input strings they crossed; and **this implementation rebuilds 29 of 31 of those strings
from real send rows** — the only canary that tests our code rather than their arithmetic, and the one
the other two cannot substitute for.

**THE CAUSE OF THE SIXTEEN MISSES WAS THE SERIALISATION, AND IT IS THE ODD ONE OUT IN THIS DISTRICT.**
Python's `json.dumps` DEFAULT separators — `", "` and `": "`, with spaces — where every other digest
here uses R729's compact form. Sixteen reasonable encodings all missed because the working one is the
one nobody would guess in a codebase whose every other hash is compact. Their prose spec named the
six FIELDS and not the SERIALISATION; **they had registered that exact defect the same day, dropped
a glyph hash for it, and then shipped a door spec carrying it** — their words: *the rule was
registered and the way of making it was not removed.* A rule that removes only the instance leaves
the method in place.

**AND THE HALF THAT WAS OURS: `JSON.parse` DESTROYS A DISTINCTION PYTHON KEEPS.** `str()` of a float
retains its point — `20.0`, `1.0`, `300.0` — while JavaScript's `String(20.0)` is `"20"`, and once a
file is parsed the float-ness is unrecoverable. Three worked examples differ from this implementation
on exactly that. **The failure direction is what makes it serious: a false NEGATIVE, a withdrawn row
the door cannot see, on every item whose answer is a round number.** It is a two-valued ambiguity
with a known cause, so it is ENUMERATED and not guessed — `canonicalSubstanceCandidates` returns both
spellings where `solutionValue` is a whole number. Guessing one would have made the door quietly
blind to a predictable slice of the corpus.

**THREE OF THE SIX FIELDS DO NOT EXIST IN THIS STORE.** `Item` holds `solution` (null on the rows
checked) and has no `solutionValue` and no `solutionKind` column. A serving row's substance is
therefore **not computable from this store's own data**: 335 of 507 serving rows are reported NOT
COMPUTABLE rather than hashed over a different set of fields and called the key. Where a crossed send
supplies the missing three they are RECOVERED and the recovery is declared per row. **The serving
side cannot compute the identity of what it serves**, which is a finding about this schema and not
about the notice.

## R905 — A re-pin is not a warrant from the authoring store

The door refused four serving rows, and two of them this store had earlier classed as safe **on my
own inference**: `MC01-CALC-01` and `MC01-CALC-05` were credited with a "later authority" because
they had been re-pinned against the amended source.

**A RE-PIN ASSERTS THAT A ROW IS BYTE-IDENTICAL TO WHAT THE REVIEWER VERIFIED. IT IS SILENT ON
WHETHER THE AUTHORING STORE STANDS BEHIND THOSE BYTES.** Those are different questions with different
authorities, and the notice puts both rows in the twenty-five-with-no-replacement class — no
replacement exists anywhere and nobody has ruled them back. They are out.

**What caught it was not a re-reading.** It was a door keyed on SUBSTANCE rather than on id, arming
on evidence the sender supplied. The earlier classification was careful, cited real events, and was
wrong because it answered the question it could see with the authority it had to hand.

**THE OTHER TWO ARE A CONFLICT AND STAY REPORTED.** Cowork withdrew the SUBSTANCE of `MC04-FDP-04`
and `MC05-FDP-01`; Annie restored the ROW and David endorsed keeping them. Two authorities over two
different things and this store holds neither — pulling would resolve it in favour of whoever spoke
last, which is not a rule (R867). One word settles it either way.

## R906 — Money a child reads carries its unit wherever it sits, and the two stores applied one ruling to different scopes

David's scope ruling, 2026-08-30. **This store's stems already carry it; the authoring store's do
not and are amending.**

The instructive part is how the divergence happened. Their money amender says on its face *no stem
is touched, no "pounds" becomes £ in any sentence*, applied on the reviewer's line THE UNIT'S
PRESENCE, NOT ITS SPELLING — prose-money harmonisation read as a voice question and left out. This
store applied the same ruling to stem and options together. **Neither store drifted and neither
misread a value: one ruling, two defensible scopes, and a district holding a third state.**

The consequence is mechanical and it is the reason scope has to be settled rather than tolerated:
their `replacementSubstanceSha256` values recompute exactly over THEIR current post-amendment rows,
and are **useless as a lifting key for ours**, because ours are amended at the stem as well. A
replacement digest that is accurate about one store's bytes and unusable by the other is not a
defect in either digest. **Re-check when their re-derived digests cross**; this store does not
re-amend prose to make a digest match, which would be fitting the corpus to the key.

## R907 — A serving side that cannot compute the identity of what it serves

David's ruling to register, 2026-08-30, and it is a fact about this schema rather than about any notice.

The substance of an item — the thing a withdrawal keys on — is six fields: stem, the sorted option
values, the key, `solution`, `solutionValue` and `solutionKind`. **This store holds three of them.**
`Item` has a `solution` column (null on every row inspected) and has **no `solutionValue` and no
`solutionKind` column at all.** So a serving row's identity is not computable from this store's own
data: **335 of 505 serving rows report NOT COMPUTABLE**, and the 170 that resolve do so only because
a crossed send supplies the missing three and the recovery is declared per row.

**THE CONSEQUENCE IS NOT ABOUT THIS WITHDRAWAL.** Any question of the form *is this row the same
question as that one* — a duplicate sweep, a re-import diff, a withdrawal, a shuffle audit — is
unanswerable here without borrowing half the answer from the party asking. **A store that must ask
the sender what it is serving cannot independently check the sender**, and every guard built on
substance inherits that dependency silently. The door reports the uncomputable class rather than
hashing over the three fields it has and calling that the key, which would have produced a digest
that matches nothing and refuses nothing while looking exactly like a clean screen.

The repair is a schema change and is not made here on a check's say-so. **What is closed today is
the invisibility**: the count is printed on every run, so the gap is a number rather than a
discovery.

## R908 — Re-arming: the withdrawn keys are historical and only the lifting keys move

The notice was re-derived after the stem ruling and superseded (`943abb60…` over `6774c502…`),
and the shape of the change is worth keeping. **The WITHDRAWN digests did not move — they are
computed over a retained 196-row send, which is historical and cannot change. Only the LIFTING keys
moved**, because what replaces a withdrawn row depends on current bytes and current bytes had been
amended. A door armed on the old notice went on refusing exactly what it had been refusing; it was
only the lifting half that had gone stale.

**SO THE STANDING NOTICE IS THE HEAD OF A DERIVED SUPERSESSION CHAIN, NEVER THE FIRST FILENAME.** A
superseded notice is retained rather than deleted (R888 — a record is corrected by adding to it), so
the directory holds more than one, and the first version of this door picked by `readdirSync` order.
That would have served whichever sorted first, forever, silently. Each notice names the sha256 of
the one it supersedes; the standing one is the notice nothing supersedes, and two heads or none is an
ambiguity the door refuses rather than resolving by guess.

**RESULT: 12 of 13 lifted on bytes.** The one that did not is `MC03-CALC-07`, and the cause is theirs
rather than ours: their declared replacement digest **is reproduced by their own send row, which
still carries BARE option values** (`24.00`) while its stem is amended. Under the ruling — a money
amount a child reads carries its unit wherever it sits — this store's row is the correct form and
their re-derivation missed the values on that single row. **A lifting key that describes a row nobody
holds does not lift anything**, and the only way to tell that from a serving-side fault is to
recompute both sides, which is what the canaries make possible.

**AND THE TWO REFUSALS BECAME RULED EXCEPTIONS, NOT SILENT SKIPS.** `MC04-FDP-04` and `MC05-FDP-01`
carry a withdrawn substance and a later ruling that permits them. The exception is recorded keyed on
SUBSTANCE, exactly as the withdrawal is, naming the authority that granted it — and printed on every
run. **An exception that stops being visible stops being a decision** (R601); the sender's own note
says *nothing chose between them*, and what is different now is that something did, with the unchosen
variant retained on the row so the choice is inspectable rather than remembered.

## R909 — A row serves on identity, reading and authorship, or it waits

Annie's 195th, and it is the district's operating sentence.

**A PIN ASSERTS IDENTITY. A VERDICT ASSERTS READING. THE AUTHOR STANDING BEHIND THE BYTES IS A THIRD
THING NEITHER SUPPLIES.** She wrote the first two clauses in her signature scoping (R877); the door
enforced the third before anyone had named it. `MC01-CALC-01` and `MC01-CALC-05` carried her
verification and their pins and carried **no author's re-issue after the send that shipped them was
withdrawn** — her words: *they served on soundness without authority, which is a different lack than
the six had and the same exit.*

**THAT IS THE PRECISE SHAPE OF MY ERROR AT R905.** I credited those two with a "later authority"
because they had been re-pinned. A re-pin is an IDENTITY assertion; withdrawal is an AUTHORSHIP
question; and I answered the second with the first because both are true statements about the same
row. **Two of the three assertions were in hand and the missing one was the one at issue** — which is
why the fault survived a careful reading and fell to a door keyed on the right thing.

**THE RETURN PATH IS PAVED AND IT IS ASYMMETRIC.** The author re-issues through the gate, and where
the re-issued bytes are byte-identical to the pinned ones, her verdicts RE-ATTACH — because a reading
is of bytes and survives their re-issue. Her sentence: **authority arrives fresh; the reading never
left.** So a withdrawal costs an author's re-issue and never a re-review, provided the bytes come
back identical. Nothing here re-reads what has not changed.

## R910 — A refusal answered by completing an amendment, not by judging a form

This store refused to convert *1 pound 50* to *£1.50* on the ground that converting a written form is
a ruling. **It is, and the ruling already existed.** Her 180th amended that stem's SERVING bytes to
£1.50 and signed against the pin; what had never happened was the amendment reaching the SOURCE. So
the disposition is not a fresh form judgement but **her amendment completing its journey**: the
authoring slot amends to byte-identity with the ruled serving stem, under both-or-neither.

**THE GROUND MATTERS MORE THAN THE OUTCOME HERE.** She names a second reason the slot text is wrong —
spoken register transcribed rather than prose or symbol, no form a child should meet in print — and
then explicitly declines to rest on it: *the ground of the amendment is the 180th's authority, not a
new taste.* **A ruling that arrives with two grounds and names which one carries it can be applied by
somebody who disagrees with the other**, and it cannot be over-extended into a taste rule about
transcribed speech that nobody made.

The refusal was right and the answer was not a reversal. **A store that refuses correctly should
expect the reply to be an authority it did not know about at least as often as a concession** — the
refusal is what surfaced the gap between a ruled serving text and an unruled source.

## R911 — A pending lift is a state, not a silence

`MC03-CALC-07` matches neither the withdrawn substance nor the declared replacement: this store's row
is not the withdrawn one, so nothing refuses, and the sender's lifting key does not describe it, so
nothing lifts. **Until today the door reported that as "not named in any standing withdrawal" —
indistinguishable from a row the notice never mentioned.**

A row NAMED with a replacement that does not describe it is a third state and now has a name,
`AWAITING RE-DERIVATION`. The cause is on the sender's side and is checkable rather than asserted:
their v3 replacement digest is reproduced by their own send row, which still carries BARE option
values while its stem is amended. **It lifts mechanically the moment their re-derivation describes
the row, and the door reports it on the next run** — which is what makes "report when it lifts" a
mechanism rather than a thing somebody remembers to do.

## R912 — Where a conversion is the skill, notation distance is the work

Annie's 196th, and it closes both open lines by ruling that neither is a fault.

**The pence gap between `MC02-RP-02`'s stem and its options is not a seam; it is the task.** The item
is a rate item: the child takes a shop price in pounds, finds a per-apple price in pence, and
compares. **The pounds-to-pence step is part of the work the item exists to ask**, and the corpus
says so in its own voice — `MC03-RP-01` runs the same crossing in the other direction, a pence stem
with a pounds key. **Smoothing the distance would do the child's first step for her: the
supplied-retrieval fault wearing a currency.**

**THE GENERAL FORM, AND IT REACHES BEYOND MONEY.** Any surface difference between a stem and its
options is either noise or the exercise, and only the item's own purpose decides which. A
consistency sweep cannot tell them apart, because a sweep sees a difference and a difference is what
a conversion item is FOR. **So a notation-harmonising pass must ask what each item tests before it
harmonises anything**, or it will quietly delete the skill from every item whose skill it is.

**AND THE TWO NOT-CHECKED LINES CLOSE AS DESIGN, NOT AS DEBT.** The `solution` field keeps its bare
pence: it is a machine-read check line, **its reader is the checker, and the checker is the one
reader for whom units are noise** — the child's-eye rule governs what a CHILD reads and does not
reach a field no child meets. Mixed money notation corpus-wide is not a fault population either:
where the mixing is the item's task it is design, and the units rule governs PRESENCE of units, which
is whole. **Nothing to sweep** — and a not-checked line answered as design is closed, where the same
line left open is a permanent invitation to somebody's tidy-up.

She also states the grounds she did NOT rest on, again: leave-it fails on VOICE (spoken register
transcribed, one stem in a private notation is a cost with no buyer) and `150p` fails on THE WORLD
(shop prices are not written that way, and a stem should not teach a form the high street never
shows). **The precedent settled it and the reasons are given so the choice is a reading and not an
